life-citizen-india.title: Citizen India: documents, rights and complaints
life-citizen-india.description: Get and protect your Aadhaar, PAN, voter ID, passport, driving licence and DigiLocker; file an FIR, RTI or consumer complaint; vote and get your local government to act.

courses.title: Your documents: Aadhaar, PAN, voter ID, passport, DL, DigiLocker
courses.summary: What each key Indian document is for, how to apply or update it through official portals, and how to keep it safe from misuse and fake websites.

lessons.title: Aadhaar and PAN: identity and tax

scenes.text: Pooja, 18, in Patna gives full Aadhaar photocopies to a sim shop, a coaching centre and a hostel — without writing anything on them.
Months later she finds two mobile connections she never took, registered in her name.
Her uncle shows her how to check connections on Sanchar Saathi, download masked Aadhaar and lock biometrics on myAadhaar.
She also gets her PAN online in minutes for her first part-time job and links it with Aadhaar.

steps.title: Aadhaar: what it is (and isn’t)
steps.body:
- A **12-digit** identity number issued by **UIDAI**, linked to your demographic details (name, date of birth, address) and biometrics (fingerprints, iris, photo).
- Enrolment is **free**. Residents of India, including children, can enrol.
- It is **proof of identity** (and address as updated), but the Aadhaar Act says it is **not proof of citizenship or domicile**.
- Children’s biometrics must be updated at about **5 and 15 years** of age.
- Update address and some details online via the official **myAadhaar** portal; biometric changes need an Aadhaar centre.

steps.title: Keep Aadhaar safe
steps.body:
- Use **masked Aadhaar** (only last 4 digits visible) when someone needs a copy.
- On any photocopy, write the **purpose and date** (e.g., ‘For hostel admission only, 12/07’) across it.
- **Lock your biometrics** on myAadhaar or mAadhaar; unlock temporarily when needed.
- Check **Aadhaar authentication history** on myAadhaar for unknown use.
- Use an **offline Aadhaar QR / e-KYC** instead of photocopies where accepted.
- Never share Aadhaar OTPs.

steps.title: PAN: your tax identity
steps.body:
- **PAN** (Permanent Account Number) is a **10-character** alphanumeric ID issued by the **Income Tax Department** (e.g., ABCDE1234F format).
- Needed for filing income tax, opening many bank and investment accounts, and high-value transactions.
- Apply through the authorised portals (Protean/NSDL or UTIITSL) using Form 49A, or get a free **instant e-PAN** using Aadhaar on the income-tax e-filing portal.
- **Link PAN with Aadhaar** — an unlinked PAN can become inoperative.
- One person, **one PAN** only. Having more than one can attract a penalty; surrender extra PANs.

steps.title: Fake portals and agents
steps.body: Many websites look official and charge extra fees, or steal data. Always type the address yourself or start from the government’s official sites (they usually end in **.gov.in** — e.g., uidai.gov.in, incometax.gov.in). Ignore SMS links claiming ‘Aadhaar suspended’ or ‘PAN blocked — click to update’.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Log in to myAadhaar: download your masked Aadhaar, check authentication history, and lock biometrics. Check on the e-filing portal that your PAN-Aadhaar link status is ‘linked’.

lessons.title: Voter ID and passport

scenes.text: Imtiaz turns 18 in Srinagar. He assumes he’ll get a voter card automatically.
His teacher shows the class how to fill Form 6 on the Voter Helpline app. Imtiaz is added to the electoral roll and gets his EPIC.
A year later he gets a college exchange offer to Japan. He applies for a passport on the official Passport Seva portal.
After his appointment and police verification, the passport arrives by post. He avoided agents who wanted to charge him triple.

steps.title: Voter registration
steps.body:
- Any **Indian citizen aged 18** or more on the **qualifying date** can register in the constituency where they ordinarily live. There are now four qualifying dates a year (1 January, 1 April, 1 July, 1 October), and **17-year-olds can apply in advance**.
- Apply with **Form 6** on the official voters’ service portal or the **Voter Helpline app** of the Election Commission of India (ECI).
- You get an **EPIC** (Electors Photo Identity Card).
- **Form 8**: corrections, shifting residence, replacement EPIC. Your area’s **BLO** (Booth Level Officer) can help.
- What matters on polling day is that **your name is on the electoral roll**; if you lack your EPIC, ECI notifies other photo IDs you can show.

steps.title: Passport: the official route
steps.body:
1. Register on the official **Passport Seva** portal or mPassport Seva app (Ministry of External Affairs).
2. Fill the application (fresh/re-issue; normal or **Tatkaal** for urgent cases).
3. Pay the fee online and book an appointment at a **Passport Seva Kendra (PSK)** or **Post Office PSK**.
4. Visit with **original documents** (proof of date of birth, address, ID as listed on the portal).
5. **Police verification** (before or after issue depending on case).
6. Track status online; passport is sent by post.
An adult’s ordinary passport is generally valid for **10 years**; minors’ passports have shorter validity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using **look-alike passport websites** that charge extra ‘service fees’ — always use the official portal.
- Name or date-of-birth **mismatch** across documents (Aadhaar, school certificate, PAN). Fix mismatches first; they cause delays.
- Giving wrong address details — police verification fails.
- Forgetting to renew a passport before it has less than 6 months validity (many countries require 6 months).

steps.title: Keep a ‘document consistency’ sheet
steps.body: Write down exactly how your name, date of birth, father’s/mother’s name and address appear on each document. Use the **same spelling** everywhere. If you change your name (e.g., after marriage), plan the updates in order and keep the official proof (marriage certificate or gazette notification).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Search your name on the ECI electoral roll search service. If you’re 17+, find Form 6 on the Voter Helpline app.

lessons.title: Driving licence: from learner to licensed

scenes.text: Sunaina, 18, in Raipur has been riding her brother’s scooter ‘just around the colony’ without a licence.
A traffic check stops her. Her father has to pay a fine as the owner and is told it could have been much worse.
She applies for a learner’s licence on the official Sarathi Parivahan portal, takes the online road-rules test, and practises with her father for a month.
She passes the driving test at the RTO and downloads her DL into DigiLocker.

steps.title: Age rules
steps.body:
- **16 years**: learner’s licence for a **gearless motorcycle up to 50 cc**, with the consent of a parent/guardian.
- **18 years**: licence for other non-transport vehicles (motorcycles with gear, cars).
- Transport (commercial) vehicles have additional age and eligibility requirements.
Driving without a valid licence is an offence; under the amended Motor Vehicles Act, if a juvenile commits a traffic offence, the guardian or vehicle owner can be held responsible.

steps.title: Step by step
steps.body:
1. **Learner’s licence (LL)**: apply on the official **Sarathi Parivahan** portal (Ministry of Road Transport and Highways); upload documents, pay fee.
2. Take the **LL test** on road signs and rules — many states allow an online test with Aadhaar authentication; others at the RTO.
3. LL is valid for **6 months**. Practise only with a licensed driver beside you and ‘L’ plates displayed.
4. After at least **30 days** from the LL, apply for the **driving licence (DL)** and book a driving test slot.
5. Pass the practical test at the RTO (or as permitted in your state).
6. DL is issued; keep it in DigiLocker/mParivahan too.

steps.title: Prepare well
steps.body: Study the traffic signs (mandatory, cautionary, informatory), right of way, lane discipline and signals. For the practical test, practise slow-speed control, figure-of-8 (two-wheelers), reversing and parking (cars), mirror checks and indicators. Show calm, safe habits — examiners look for them.

steps.title: Avoid touts and fakes
steps.body: Pay only the official fees on the portal. ‘Licence without test’ offers are illegal and dangerous. Renew your DL before it expires (renewal can be applied online). Update the address on your DL when you move.

steps.title: Other countries
steps.body: Indian licences may be used abroad in some places with an **International Driving Permit (IDP)**, issued by the RTO. Rules vary by country — check the destination country’s official guidance before driving there.

quiz.q: Minimum age for a car licence (non-transport)?
quiz.why: 18 years.

quiz.why: Only the official process is valid.

lessons.title: DigiLocker, UMANG and keeping documents safe

scenes.text: When floods hit Chennai, the Raman family’s cupboard is soaked — marksheets, RC book and certificates ruined.
Their neighbour, Mr. Iyer, had linked his family’s Aadhaar to DigiLocker and pulled in their licences, marksheets and vehicle papers.
He uses the DigiLocker copies for insurance and bank work the following week.
The Ramans now keep digital copies, a waterproof pouch of originals and a list of document numbers.

steps.title: What DigiLocker is
steps.body: **DigiLocker** is the Government of India’s digital document wallet (under the Ministry of Electronics and IT). You sign up with your mobile number and Aadhaar, then **pull** documents directly from issuers: driving licence, vehicle RC, CBSE and many state-board marksheets, Aadhaar, PAN, insurance policies and more. Under the IT Act rules for digital lockers, documents **issued** into DigiLocker by the issuing authority are treated as equivalent to the original physical documents. (Your own uploaded scans are just copies.)

steps.title: UMANG and other official apps
steps.body:
- **UMANG**: one app for many central and state services (EPF passbook, some utility payments, scheme information).
- **mParivahan**: virtual DL and RC.
- **mAadhaar**: Aadhaar services.
- **Voter Helpline**: electoral services.
Download only from official app stores, checking the developer (e.g., the ministry or NIC/NeGD).

steps.title: A family document system
steps.body:
1. **Originals** in one waterproof, fire-resistant folder (birth certificates, property papers, marksheets, passports, policy documents).
2. **Digital**: DigiLocker for issued documents + encrypted scans of the rest.
3. **A master list** (paper and digital): document name, number, issue date, expiry date, where kept.
4. **Expiry reminders**: passport, DL, insurance, PUC.
5. Tell a trusted family member where things are.

steps.title: Privacy matters
steps.body: Never share DigiLocker login or OTP. Share documents only with trusted organisations and for a specific purpose. Don’t keep photos of all your IDs in your phone gallery or chat apps where they can be leaked.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: Procedures and portals change from time to time. Always follow the latest instructions on the official .gov.in website. This is general education, not legal advice.

courses.title: Getting justice: FIR, RTI and consumer complaints
courses.summary: How to file an FIR (including Zero FIR and e-FIR) under the BNSS, what to do if police refuse, how to use the RTI Act, and how to win a consumer complaint — with India’s grievance portals.
outcomes: Learners can file an FIR and know their rights under the BNSS
Learners know the steps if police refuse to register an FIR
Learners can draft and appeal an RTI application
Learners can resolve a consumer dispute via 1915 and the consumer commissions
Learners can choose the right grievance channel (bank, insurance, government)
courses.guardianNote: Explains, in a factual and non-graphic way, how ordinary citizens report crimes and complaints to police, government and consumer bodies. It mentions crime only in general terms. Knowing these rights helps young people and their families act safely and lawfully.

lessons.title: Filing an FIR: your rights at the police station

scenes.text: Anil’s motorcycle is stolen outside a market in Meerut. At the police station, he is told to ‘come back tomorrow’ and that it’s ‘not our area’.
His cousin Farah, a law student, explains: theft is a cognizable offence; any police station must register at least a Zero FIR and transfer it.
Anil calmly asks for his statement to be recorded, reads it before signing, and receives a free copy of the FIR.
Farah also shows him that many states allow e-FIRs for vehicle theft online.

steps.title: Today’s laws
steps.body: Since **1 July 2024**, India’s criminal laws are the **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS)** (offences), the **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS)** (procedure) and the **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA)** (evidence). They replaced the IPC, CrPC and Indian Evidence Act. FIR rules are now in **Section 173 of the BNSS**.

steps.title: What an FIR is
steps.body:
An **FIR (First Information Report)** is the written record of information about a **cognizable offence** — a serious offence where police can arrest without a warrant and must investigate (e.g., theft, assault, robbery, cheating, kidnapping, sexual offences). Key points under BNSS Section 173:
- Information can be given **orally, in writing or electronically**. Oral information is written down and read over to you.
- An e-FIR/electronic information must be **signed by you within three days** to be taken on record.
- **Zero FIR**: you can report at **any police station**, regardless of where the crime happened; it is then transferred to the right station.
- You get a **free copy** of the FIR.
- For certain offences against women, statements are recorded by a woman officer, and special protections apply.

steps.title: What to say and check
steps.body:
Give: your name and contact, **what happened, when, where**, who was involved (names/descriptions), witnesses, property details (e.g., vehicle number, chassis/engine number, IMEI for phones), and any evidence (CCTV location, photos, messages).
Before signing: **read it fully**; make sure facts are correct and nothing is added that you didn’t say. Note the **FIR number, date and police station**. Keep calm and polite; ask for the officer’s name.

steps.title: If police refuse to register
steps.body:
1. Send the information in writing (by post/email) to the **Superintendent of Police / Commissioner** (BNSS Section 173(4)). Keep proof.
2. If still not registered, you may apply to the **Judicial Magistrate** (BNSS Section 175(3)), who can direct investigation.
3. For some offences punishable with 3–7 years’ imprisonment, BNSS allows police to do a **preliminary enquiry** (up to 14 days) before registering, with senior officer permission.
4. **Non-cognizable** offences (e.g., minor ones) are recorded differently; police need a magistrate’s order to investigate — they should still record your information and guide you.
For cyber fraud, call **1930** and file at **cybercrime.gov.in**.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. For serious matters, contact a lawyer or free legal aid through Legal Services Authorities (NALSA helpline **15100**). In an emergency, call **112**.

a.text: Your phone was snatched near a bus stand in another police area. The nearest station officer says, ‘Not our jurisdiction, go there.’

quiz.q: Which law contains FIR rules today?
quiz.why: BNSS replaced the CrPC from 1 July 2024.

quiz.q: A Zero FIR can be filed…
quiz.why: It’s then transferred.

quiz.q: Is the FIR copy free for the informant?
quiz.why: A free copy must be given.

quiz.q: Police refuse to register an FIR for a cognizable offence. First escalation?

quiz.why: BNSS Section 173(4).

quiz.q: An e-FIR must be signed by the informant within…
quiz.why: BNSS Section 173(1)(ii).

lessons.title: RTI: asking the government for information

story.title: Where did the road money go?

scenes.text: In a village in Rajasthan, a road was ‘completed’ on paper, but villagers still walk through mud.
Kamla Devi, a self-help-group leader, files an RTI asking for the sanctioned amount, contractor name, completion certificate and measurement book copies.
With no reply in 30 days, she files a first appeal. The documents arrive soon after.
The gram sabha discusses the gaps publicly; the work is redone. Information became power.

steps.title: The Right to Information Act 2005
steps.body:
Any **citizen of India** can request information from a **public authority** (government departments, local bodies, public sector bodies, and bodies substantially funded by government).
- Apply to the **Public Information Officer (PIO)** of that authority, in writing or online.
- **No need to give reasons** for asking.
- **Fee**: ₹10 for central government authorities (states set their own fees); **BPL** card holders are exempt.
- **Reply within 30 days**; within **48 hours** if it concerns someone’s **life or liberty**.
- Central ministries and many departments accept applications on the official **RTI Online** portal; many states have their own portals.

steps.title: Writing a good RTI
steps.body:
- Ask for **specific records**, not opinions: ‘Please provide certified copies of the work order, measurement book entries and completion certificate for the road from X to Y sanctioned in 2023–24’ — not ‘Why is the road bad?’
- Number your questions; keep them few and clear.
- Mention the period and location.
- Ask for inspection of files if useful.
- Keep copies of your application and fee proof.

steps.title: Appeals
steps.body:
- **First appeal**: if there’s no reply in 30 days or you’re unsatisfied, appeal to the **First Appellate Authority** (a senior officer in the same authority) within **30 days**.
- **Second appeal**: to the **Central or State Information Commission** within **90 days** of the first appeal decision (or the date it was due).
- Commissions can order disclosure and impose penalties on PIOs for unjustified delay or refusal.

steps.title: What can be refused
steps.body: Section 8 lists exemptions, such as information affecting national security or sovereignty, certain personal information with no public interest, information that would impede investigation, and cabinet papers before decisions. Even so, information that cannot be denied to Parliament or a State Legislature cannot be denied to a citizen. Private companies are not covered directly, but information about them held by a public authority (e.g., a regulator) may be.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. Rules on fees and formats vary by state; check the relevant official portal.

lessons.title: Consumer complaints: from helpline to commission

scenes.text: Six weeks after buying a refrigerator in Jalandhar, Gurpreet’s compressor fails. The company keeps ‘escalating’ but never repairs it.
He registers a grievance with the National Consumer Helpline (1915). The company is contacted, but still no fix.
He files a complaint online with the District Consumer Commission, attaching the bill, warranty card and emails. No lawyer needed.
The commission orders replacement plus compensation for harassment and litigation costs.

steps.title: Your rights under the Consumer Protection Act 2019
steps.body: The Act protects anyone who buys goods or services for personal use (online or offline). Your rights include: **safety**, **information** (price, quality, quantity), **choice**, being **heard**, **redressal**, and **consumer education**. Problems covered include **defective goods**, **deficient services**, **unfair trade practices** (e.g., misleading claims), charging above MRP, and misleading advertisements. The Act also covers **e-commerce** and **product liability**.

steps.title: Step-by-step
steps.body:
1. **Complain to the seller/company in writing** (email, app, customer care) — keep ticket numbers.
2. Register with the **National Consumer Helpline: 1915**, the NCH app, or WhatsApp/website. NCH tries to resolve it with the company (a pre-litigation step).
3. If unresolved, send a **written notice** giving a deadline.
4. File a complaint with the **Consumer Commission** — online through the official e-Daakhil/e-Jagriti system or in person. You can file where **you live or work**, not only where the seller is.
5. Attach: bill/invoice, warranty, photos, emails, chat screenshots, and your requested relief (refund, replacement, compensation).

steps.title: Which commission?
steps.body:
Based on the **value of goods or services paid**:
- **District Commission**: up to ₹50 lakh
- **State Commission**: above ₹50 lakh and up to ₹2 crore
- **National Commission**: above ₹2 crore
Complaints generally must be filed within **2 years** of the problem arising. You can appear **yourself** — a lawyer isn’t required. Fees are small, and for low-value claims (up to ₹5 lakh) there is no fee.

steps.title: Other complaint channels
steps.body:
- **Banks/NBFCs/digital payments**: bank’s grievance cell, then **RBI Integrated Ombudsman** (online complaint management system).
- **Insurance**: insurer’s grievance cell, then IRDAI’s **Bima Bharosa** or the **Insurance Ombudsman**.
- **Investments**: SEBI **SCORES**.
- **Central government departments**: **CPGRAMS** (public grievance portal).
- **Telecom**: provider’s grievance and appellate channels.
Always keep reference numbers.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. Limits and procedures may be updated; check the official consumer affairs portals.

lessons.title: Free legal aid and writing an effective complaint

scenes.text: Shanta, a construction worker in Pune, hasn’t been paid for two months. She thinks lawyers are only for the rich.
A volunteer at a community centre tells her about free legal aid and the NALSA helpline 15100.
A paralegal helps her write a clear complaint with dates, amounts and witness names to the labour department.
The contractor is called for a hearing and pays her dues.

steps.title: Free legal aid in India
steps.body: Under the **Legal Services Authorities Act 1987**, free legal services are available through **NALSA** (national), **State**, **District** and **Taluk** Legal Services Authorities. Eligible groups include women and children, members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, persons with disabilities, victims of trafficking or disasters, industrial workmen, people in custody, and people below a set income limit. Services include advice, a lawyer, drafting and **Lok Adalats** (for settling disputes amicably). NALSA helpline: **15100**.

steps.title: The 5-part complaint letter
steps.body:
1. **To**: correct officer/authority and address.
2. **Subject**: one line (‘Complaint regarding non-payment of wages for May–June 2025’).
3. **Facts**: in date order — what, when, where, who, amounts.
4. **Evidence**: list attachments (bills, photos, messages, witness names).
5. **Request**: exactly what you want (payment, refund, action) and a reasonable deadline.
Sign, date, keep a copy, and get an acknowledgement (stamp, email reply or reference number).

steps.title: Tone and follow-up
steps.body: Be factual and polite; avoid insults or exaggeration — they weaken your case. Follow up on the date you mentioned. Escalate step by step: officer → senior officer → appellate/grievance authority → ombudsman/commission/court.

steps.title: Avoid
steps.body:
- Paying ‘agents’ who promise quick results through contacts.
- Signing blank papers or documents you don’t understand.
- Missing deadlines (limitation periods).
- Sharing only on social media instead of official channels.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. For your specific situation, contact your District Legal Services Authority or a lawyer.

courses.title: Being an active citizen: vote, local government, rights and duties
courses.summary: How voting works (EVM, VVPAT, NOTA), how panchayats and municipalities work and how to get things fixed, your Fundamental Rights and Duties, and the helplines every Indian should know.
outcomes: Learners can describe the voting process and tools like VVPAT, NOTA and cVIGIL
Learners can explain the roles of gram sabha, panchayat and municipality
Learners can name the six groups of Fundamental Rights and some Fundamental Duties
Learners can raise a civic complaint effectively
Learners know India’s key helplines

lessons.title: How voting works

scenes.text: Rukmini Nani, 82, in Mysuru has voted in every election since she was young. This year she takes her grandson Kiran, voting for the first time.
At the booth, an officer checks Kiran’s name in the roll, marks his finger with indelible ink and he signs the register.
He presses the button next to his chosen candidate on the EVM and watches the VVPAT window show the slip for 7 seconds.
Outside, Nani says: ‘Your one vote counts exactly as much as a minister’s.’

steps.title: Before polling day
steps.body:
- Check your name in the **electoral roll** (ECI services portal or Voter Helpline app) and find your **polling station**.
- Learn about candidates: ECI publishes candidate **affidavits** (criminal cases, assets, education) — see the ‘Know Your Candidate’ information.
- The **Model Code of Conduct** applies from the announcement of elections; citizens can report violations (like distributing cash or liquor) through ECI’s **cVIGIL** app.

steps.title: At the polling booth
steps.body:
1. Stand in the queue (separate queues may exist; senior citizens and persons with disabilities get facilitation).
2. First polling officer checks your name and ID.
3. Second officer marks your **left forefinger with indelible ink**, you sign/thumb the register, and get a slip.
4. Third officer activates the **EVM** ballot unit.
5. Press the blue button next to your choice; a beep confirms.
6. The **VVPAT** shows a printed slip with the candidate’s serial number, name and symbol for about 7 seconds, then it drops into a sealed box.
Your vote is **secret**. Phones are generally not allowed inside the booth.

steps.title: NOTA
steps.body: **NOTA (None of the Above)** has been on EVMs since 2013 after a Supreme Court judgment. It lets you formally record that you reject all candidates. Under current rules, the candidate with the most votes still wins even if NOTA gets more votes; NOTA is a way to express your view while keeping your vote secret.

steps.title: Voting well
steps.body: Judge candidates on their record, promises you can check, and integrity — not on gifts, caste or religion appeals. Accepting money or gifts for votes is an electoral offence. Encourage first-time voters and help elders get to the booth.

activity.prompt: Put the polling-booth steps in order.
items: Officer checks your name in the roll and your ID
Indelible ink on your left forefinger and signature in the register
Press the button next to your choice
Check the VVPAT slip shown for about 7 seconds

quiz.q: VVPAT lets a voter…
options: See a printed slip confirming their choice
quiz.why: Verification of the vote.

quiz.q: NOTA means…
quiz.why: Option to reject all candidates.

quiz.q: Which app lets citizens report Model Code of Conduct violations?
quiz.why: ECI’s citizen vigilance app.

quiz.q: Accepting money for your vote is…
quiz.why: Bribery at elections is illegal.

sources: PUCL v. Union of India (2013) — NOTA

lessons.title: Local government: getting the streetlight fixed

scenes.text: In a ward of Bhopal, the lane to the bus stop has been dark for months. Girls avoid it after 7 pm.
College student Ayaan photographs the broken poles, notes their numbers and files a complaint on the municipal corporation’s app.
When nothing happens, he and neighbours attend the ward committee meeting with a signed letter and photos, and meet their councillor.
Two weeks later the lights are repaired. They keep the complaint number to report if it fails again.

steps.title: Three levels of government
steps.body:
- **Union** (central) government — defence, railways, currency, etc.
- **State** governments — police, health, agriculture, etc.
- **Local** governments — created as constitutional bodies by the **73rd (panchayats)** and **74th (municipalities) Amendments of 1992**.
Rural areas generally have a three-tier **Panchayati Raj** (gram panchayat, block/panchayat samiti, zila parishad). Urban areas have **municipal corporations**, **municipal councils** and **nagar panchayats**, divided into **wards** with elected councillors. Seats are reserved for women, SCs and STs (at least one-third for women; many states reserve 50%).

steps.title: Gram sabha and ward committees
steps.body: The **gram sabha** is all registered voters of a village panchayat area. It can discuss plans, approve beneficiary lists and conduct **social audits** of schemes like MGNREGA. In cities, **ward committees** and **area sabhas** (where states have created them) let residents raise issues. Attending these meetings is one of the most powerful things a citizen can do.

steps.title: Getting a civic problem fixed
steps.body:
1. **Identify** the responsible body (municipality for streetlights, garbage, drains; state electricity board for power supply; PWD for some roads).
2. **Document**: photos, exact location, pole numbers, dates.
3. **Complain** on the official app/helpline/portal; note the complaint number.
4. **Follow up** after the promised time; escalate to the ward officer or councillor.
5. **Organise**: a joint letter from residents carries weight.
6. **RTI** if needed to learn the status or budget.
7. For central government departments, use **CPGRAMS**.

steps.title: Be a constructive citizen
steps.body: Be specific and polite, propose solutions, and say thank you when things work. Combine complaints with your own action: segregate waste, don’t dump debris, report water leaks, plant and protect trees.

activity.prompt: Match the problem to who is usually responsible.
pairs: Garbage not collected in a city ward
Approving MGNREGA social audit in a village

quiz.q: Which amendment created constitutional status for panchayats?
quiz.why: 73rd Amendment, 1992.

quiz.q: The gram sabha consists of…
options: All registered voters of the village panchayat area
quiz.why: It’s the village assembly.

quiz.q: Best first step for a broken streetlight?
options: Complain on the official municipal app/helpline with photos and note the number
quiz.why: Documented official complaints can be tracked.

quiz.q: CPGRAMS is for grievances against…
quiz.why: Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System.

sources: Constitution of India — Parts IX and IXA

lessons.title: Fundamental Rights and Fundamental Duties

scenes.text: Lakshmi, 13, from a fishing family in Kanyakumari, is told by a private school guard that ‘children like you don’t study here’.
Her civics teacher explains the right to equality and the Right to Education, including reserved seats in many private schools for children from weaker sections.
With help from a local NGO, her mother applies through the official admission process. Lakshmi gets a seat.
In class, Lakshmi reads the Fundamental Duties and volunteers for a beach clean-up — ‘rights and duties go together’.

steps.title: Six groups of Fundamental Rights (Part III)
steps.body:
1. **Right to Equality** (Articles 14–18): equality before law, no discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth, equal opportunity in public jobs, abolition of untouchability.
2. **Right to Freedom** (19–22): speech and expression, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession (with reasonable restrictions); **Article 21** — life and personal liberty; **21A** — free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14; protection in arrest.
3. **Right against Exploitation** (23–24): no trafficking or forced labour; no child labour in hazardous work.
4. **Right to Freedom of Religion** (25–28).
5. **Cultural and Educational Rights** (29–30).
6. **Right to Constitutional Remedies** (32): approach the Supreme Court for enforcement (High Courts under Article 226).

steps.title: Rights have limits
steps.body: Most rights have **reasonable restrictions** — for example, free speech doesn’t include defamation, incitement to violence or threats. Rights mostly protect you against the **State**; some, like the ban on untouchability and child labour, also apply to private persons. Courts have interpreted Article 21 widely to include rights like privacy, dignity, a clean environment and legal aid.

steps.title: Fundamental Duties (Article 51A)
steps.body: Added in 1976, with an 11th duty in 2002. They include: respect the Constitution, the National Flag and Anthem; uphold unity and integrity; promote harmony and renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women; protect the environment and have compassion for living creatures; develop scientific temper and the spirit of inquiry; safeguard public property and abjure violence; strive towards excellence; and (for parents/guardians) provide opportunities for education to children aged 6–14.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. If your rights are violated, you can seek help from legal aid (NALSA 15100), human rights commissions, child rights commissions, or the courts.

quiz.q: Fundamental Duties are in…
quiz.why: Part IVA.

quiz.why: Right to constitutional remedies.

lessons.title: Helplines every Indian should know

scenes.text: After a confusing night when her grandfather fell and the family didn’t know whom to call, Divya, 14, in Siliguri makes a list for the fridge.
She checks every number on official websites and adds what each is for.
Months later, her grandfather receives a ‘digital arrest’ call. He looks at the list and calls 1930 instead of paying.
Divya’s list now hangs in every flat on her floor.

steps.body:

- **1906**: LPG emergency

steps.body: Add personal numbers: family doctor, nearest hospital, local police station, building security, a neighbour, and an out-of-town relative. Save them in your phone **and** on paper. Teach children to dial 112 and say their address.

life-safety-firstaid.title: Safety & first aid
life-safety-firstaid.description: Call 112, do CPR, help someone choking, stop bleeding, cool a burn, handle snakebites and dog bites, survive fire, earthquake and flood, and stay safe on Indian roads.

courses.title: First aid that saves lives
courses.summary: The first minutes matter most. Learn to check safety and call 112, give CPR, clear choking, control bleeding, cool burns, and handle snakebites, dog bites and heatstroke — with myths busted.
outcomes: Learners can follow Danger–Response–Send for help–Airway–Breathing–CPR
Learners can give hands-only CPR at the right rate and depth
Learners can help a choking adult, child and infant
Learners can control bleeding and cool a burn correctly
Learners can explain snakebite do’s and don’ts and rabies prevention

lessons.title: The first minute: check, call 112, act

scenes.text: At a bus stop in Bhubaneswar, an elderly man suddenly falls. A crowd forms but everyone just watches.
Sixteen-year-old Ritika, who learned first aid at school, checks for traffic, taps his shoulders and shouts, ‘Uncle, can you hear me?’
She points at a man: ‘You in the blue shirt — call 112, tell them a man is unconscious at the Rasulgarh bus stop.’
She checks his breathing. He is breathing normally, so she turns him into the recovery position and stays with him until the ambulance arrives.

steps.title: D-R-S-A-B-C: the order that keeps everyone safe
steps.body:
- **D — Danger**: check for traffic, fire, electricity, gas, falling objects. Don’t become a second victim.
- **R — Response**: tap the shoulders and shout. Do they answer or move?
- **S — Send for help**: call **112** (India’s single emergency number) or ask a specific person to call. Put the phone on speaker.
- **A — Airway**: tilt the head back gently and lift the chin.
- **B — Breathing**: look, listen and feel for **normal** breathing for up to 10 seconds. Occasional gasps are **not** normal breathing.
- **C — CPR**: if not breathing normally, start chest compressions (next lesson) and send for an AED (defibrillator) if one is nearby.

steps.title: Calling 112 well
steps.body:
112 connects to police, fire and ambulance services (108 or 102 also work for ambulances in many states). Say clearly:
1. **Where** you are (landmark, road, pin location — share live location if possible)
2. **What** happened
3. **How many** people hurt and their condition (conscious? breathing?)
4. Your phone number
Don’t hang up until told; they may guide you. Many phones also have an SOS shortcut (for example pressing the power button several times).

steps.title: The recovery position
steps.body:
For someone **unconscious but breathing normally** (and no suspected spine injury):
1. Kneel beside them; place the near arm at a right angle.
2. Bring the far arm across the chest, back of hand against their near cheek.
3. Bend the far knee up; pull on that knee to roll them towards you onto their side.
4. Tilt the head back to keep the airway open; mouth pointing slightly down so fluids drain.
5. Keep checking breathing until help arrives. If breathing stops, roll them back and start CPR.

steps.title: Myths that cause harm
steps.body:
- Don’t pour water into an unconscious person’s mouth — they can choke.
- Don’t make a fainted person sit up quickly or crowd them.
- Onion or shoe smelling doesn’t treat fits (seizures). For a seizure: clear the space, cushion the head, **don’t restrain and don’t put anything in the mouth**, time it, recovery position after; call 112 if it lasts more than 5 minutes, repeats, or it’s their first.
- A crowd watching is not help. **Point at one person** and give one task.

steps.title: Learn hands-on
steps.body: This course is general education, not a substitute for a certified first-aid course. Organisations like the Indian Red Cross Society and St John Ambulance run practical trainings — doing it once with a manikin makes you far more confident.

activity.prompt: Put the first-aid check in the right order.
items: Check for danger to yourself and others
Check response: tap shoulders and shout
Open the airway: head tilt, chin lift
Check for normal breathing (up to 10 seconds)
If not breathing normally, start CPR

quiz.q: India’s single emergency number is…
quiz.why: 112 connects police, fire and ambulance.

quiz.q: Why check for danger first?
options: To avoid becoming a second victim
quiz.why: An injured helper can’t help anyone.

quiz.q: An unconscious person is breathing normally. You should…
options: Place them in the recovery position and monitor
quiz.why: Recovery position keeps the airway open.

quiz.q: During a seizure you should…
options: Put a spoon in their mouth
Clear space, cushion the head, time it
quiz.why: Protect from injury; never restrain or put objects in the mouth.

quiz.q: Occasional gasps in an unresponsive person mean…
quiz.why: Agonal gasps are a sign of cardiac arrest.

sources: Indian Red Cross Society first aid manual
International first aid & resuscitation guidelines (IFRC, ILCOR)

lessons.title: CPR: push hard, push fast

scenes.text: At a Sunday match in Ludhiana, 52-year-old Mr. Gill collapses on the pitch. He doesn’t respond and is only gasping.
His nephew Harpreet calls 112 on speaker and starts pressing hard on the centre of his chest, counting aloud.
Someone remembers a song with the right beat. Two others take turns every two minutes.
The ambulance team uses a defibrillator. Mr. Gill survives. Doctors say the early CPR kept his brain alive.

steps.title: Why CPR works
steps.body: In **cardiac arrest** the heart stops pumping effectively. Without blood flow, brain damage begins within minutes. **CPR** (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) pushes blood to the brain and heart by squeezing the heart between the breastbone and spine. It buys time until a **defibrillator (AED)** and the ambulance arrive. Without CPR, the chance of survival falls rapidly with every minute.

steps.title: Hands-only CPR for an adult
steps.body:
1. Person on their back on a firm surface.
2. Heel of one hand on the **centre of the chest** (lower half of the breastbone), other hand on top, fingers interlocked.
3. Arms straight, shoulders over hands.
4. Press down **5–6 cm** and let the chest **fully come back up** each time.
5. Rate: **100–120 compressions per minute** (about two per second).
6. Don’t stop except to let an AED analyse, or if they start breathing normally, or professionals take over.
7. Swap with another helper about **every 2 minutes** — quality drops when you tire.

steps.title: Rescue breaths and AEDs
steps.body:
If you are **trained and willing**, give **30 compressions then 2 rescue breaths** (head tilt, chin lift, pinch nose, seal mouth, breathe until the chest rises, about 1 second each). If not trained or unwilling, **hands-only CPR** is far better than nothing.

**AED**: switch it on and follow the voice prompts; stick pads as shown on the pictures; make sure nobody touches the person when it says ‘analysing’ or ‘shock’. AEDs are designed for untrained people and won’t shock if it isn’t needed.

steps.title: Children and infants (if you know how)
steps.body:
- **Child** (about 1 year to puberty): one or two hands, press about **5 cm** (one-third of chest depth). Many guidelines suggest 5 initial rescue breaths if trained, then 30:2.
- **Infant** (under 1): two fingers (or two thumbs encircling) on the centre of the chest just below the nipple line, press about **4 cm** (one-third of chest depth), 100–120 per minute.
In children, arrest is often due to breathing problems, so rescue breaths matter more — another reason to take a hands-on course.

steps.title: Fears that stop people
steps.body:
- **‘I might break a rib.’** It can happen; a broken rib heals, death doesn’t.
- **‘I might be blamed.’** India’s Good Samaritan protections (Motor Vehicles Act section 134A and Supreme Court-approved guidelines) protect people who help in good faith in road emergencies, and courts generally respect good-faith rescue.
- **Pressing too gently or too slowly** is the most common mistake. Push hard and fast. Use the **CPR rhythm** lab to practise the beat.

statements.s: Adult CPR compressions should be 100–120 per minute.
statements.why: About two compressions per second.

statements.s: You should press about 1 cm deep on an adult’s chest.
statements.why: Adults need 5–6 cm to move blood.

statements.s: Hands-only CPR is useful even if you can’t give rescue breaths.
statements.why: Compressions alone circulate blood in the first minutes.

statements.s: An AED will shock anyone it is attached to, even if not needed.
statements.why: AEDs analyse the heart rhythm and only advise a shock when appropriate.

statements.s: Let the chest fully rise between compressions.
statements.why: Full recoil lets the heart refill with blood.

quiz.q: Where do you place your hands for adult CPR?
options: Centre of the chest, lower half of the breastbone
quiz.why: That’s where compressions squeeze the heart.

quiz.q: How deep for an adult?
quiz.why: Recommended depth is 5–6 cm.

quiz.q: If trained, the compression-to-breath ratio for adults is…
quiz.why: 30 compressions then 2 breaths.

quiz.q: Why swap rescuers every 2 minutes?
quiz.why: Tired rescuers press too shallow or slow.

quiz.q: When should you stop CPR?
options: When the person breathes normally, professionals take over, or the AED tells you to pause
quiz.why: Continue until one of these happens or you’re physically unable.

lessons.title: Choking: adults, children and babies

scenes.text: At a wedding lunch in Udaipur, Mr. Rathore suddenly clutches his throat. He can’t speak or cough.
A caterer, Maria, trained in first aid, asks, ‘Are you choking?’ He nods.
She leans him forward and gives firm back blows. Nothing. She switches to abdominal thrusts — on the third, a piece of food flies out.
She still advises him to see a doctor, because abdominal thrusts can cause internal injury.

steps.title: Mild vs severe choking
steps.body:
- **Mild**: the person can **cough, speak or breathe**. Encourage them to keep coughing hard. Don’t slap their back or give water yet. Stay with them.
- **Severe**: they **can’t speak, cough effectively or breathe**, may clutch the throat, go silent, turn blue. Act immediately and call 112 (or get someone to call).

steps.title: Adult or child over 1 year: back blows and abdominal thrusts
steps.body:
1. Stand slightly behind, support the chest with one hand, **lean them forward**.
2. Give up to **5 sharp back blows** between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand. Check after each.
3. If still choking: stand behind, wrap arms round their waist, make a fist just **above the navel** (below the ribs), grab it with the other hand, pull sharply **inwards and upwards** — up to **5 abdominal thrusts**.
4. Repeat 5 back blows and 5 thrusts until the object comes out or they become unresponsive.
5. If they become **unresponsive**: lower them to the floor, call 112, start **CPR**. Check the mouth for a visible object before breaths; never do blind finger sweeps.

steps.title: Babies under 1 year
steps.body:
**No abdominal thrusts for infants.**
1. Lay the baby **face down along your forearm**, head lower than chest, supporting the jaw.
2. Give up to **5 back blows** between the shoulder blades.
3. Turn the baby face up along your other arm; give up to **5 chest thrusts** with two fingers on the centre of the chest just below the nipple line.
4. Repeat until cleared or the baby becomes unresponsive — then start infant CPR and call 112.

steps.title: Special cases and after-care
steps.body:
- **Pregnant** or very large person: give **chest thrusts** (hands on the centre of the chest) instead of abdominal thrusts.
- **Alone and choking**: call 112, then press your upper abdomen hard against a chair back or table edge.
- After any abdominal thrusts, the person should be **checked by a doctor**.
- Prevention for small children: cut grapes and similar round foods lengthwise, avoid whole nuts and hard sweets for toddlers, supervise eating, keep coins, button batteries and small toy parts out of reach. **Button batteries** swallowed are an emergency — go to hospital immediately.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Giving water to a severely choking person.
- Turning a baby upside down by the legs and shaking.
- Blind finger sweeps that push the object deeper.
- Thrusts on someone who is coughing well (let them cough).

a.text: Your friend at dinner grabs her throat. You ask ‘Are you choking?’ She is coughing loudly and can speak a word.

choices.label: Encourage her to keep coughing and stay with her
choices.feedback: Correct — effective coughing is the best way to clear it.

choices.label: Immediately give abdominal thrusts
choices.feedback: Not yet — thrusts are for severe choking when coughing fails.

b.text: Now she can’t make any sound and her lips are turning blue.

choices.label: Lean her forward and give up to 5 back blows, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts; get someone to call 112
choices.feedback: Exactly right.

choices.label: Give her a glass of water
choices.feedback: Water can’t pass and may worsen things.

c.text: After the second thrust the food pops out and she breathes. What next?

choices.label: Advise a medical check-up because thrusts can cause internal injury
choices.feedback: Yes — always get checked after abdominal thrusts.

choices.label: Continue dinner, nothing else needed
choices.feedback: She’s breathing, but she should still see a doctor.

bad.text: She collapses. Lower her to the floor, call 112 and begin CPR, checking the mouth for a visible object before any breaths.

good.text: She’s safe. You recognised mild vs severe choking and acted in the right order.

lessons.title: Bleeding, burns and broken bones

scenes.text: In Kozhikode, 14-year-old Aysha’s mother slices her palm deeply while cutting jackfruit. Blood is everywhere.
Aysha presses a clean towel hard on the wound and holds the hand up, while her brother calls 112.
A week later her little cousin touches a hot tawa. Grandma reaches for toothpaste — Aysha says, ‘No! Cool water for 20 minutes.’
The doctor later tells them both actions prevented much worse injuries.

steps.title: Severe bleeding: press, don’t peek
steps.body:
1. Protect yourself (gloves or a plastic bag if available).
2. Press **firmly and directly** on the wound with a clean cloth or pad. **Keep pressure** for at least 10 minutes without lifting to check.
3. If blood soaks through, **add more cloth on top** — don’t remove the first layer.
4. Help them lie down if they feel faint; keep them warm.
5. Call 112 for heavy bleeding.
6. If an object is stuck in the wound, **don’t pull it out** — press around it.
Trained responders may use a **tourniquet** for life-threatening limb bleeding that pressure can’t control; note the time it was applied.

steps.title: Nosebleeds and small cuts
steps.body:
**Nosebleed**: sit up, **lean forward** (not back), pinch the soft part of the nose for 10–15 minutes, breathe through the mouth. Tilting the head back makes blood go down the throat. See a doctor if it lasts beyond 20 minutes, follows a head injury, or happens often.

**Small cuts**: rinse with clean running water, gentle pressure, cover with a clean dressing. Watch for infection signs (spreading redness, swelling, pus, fever). Ask a doctor about tetanus protection for dirty or deep wounds.

steps.title: Burns: cool, cover, call
steps.body:
1. **Cool** the burn under cool (not icy) **running water for 20 minutes**, as soon as possible.
2. Remove rings, watches and clothing near the burn unless stuck to the skin.
3. **Cover** loosely with cling film or a clean non-fluffy cloth.
4. Keep the person warm (cool the burn, not the whole body).
5. **Get medical help** for: burns larger than the person’s palm, any burn on face, hands, feet, genitals or joints, deep burns (white, charred, painless), electrical and chemical burns, and burns in babies, children and older adults.
**Chemical burns**: brush off dry powder, then rinse with plenty of running water for at least 20 minutes.

steps.title: Burn myths
steps.body: **Never** put ice, butter, ghee, oil, toothpaste, turmeric paste, egg white or ink on a burn. They trap heat, cause infection or damage tissue. **Don’t pop blisters** — they protect the skin underneath.

steps.title: Suspected broken bones and head injuries
steps.body:
- **Fracture signs**: pain, swelling, deformity, can’t move or bear weight. **Don’t try to straighten it.** Support it in the position found (padding, sling, rolled newspaper splint if trained); apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth; get medical help.
- **Possible neck/spine injury** (fall from height, road crash, diving): don’t move them unless in danger; keep head and neck still; call 112.
- **Head injury danger signs** — get urgent help: unconsciousness even briefly, repeated vomiting, worsening headache, confusion, drowsiness, fits, clear fluid from nose or ears, weakness on one side, unequal pupils.
This is general education, not medical advice.

lessons.title: Snakebite, dog bite and heatstroke: myths vs facts

scenes.text: In a village near Nashik, farmer Sanjay is bitten on the ankle while walking through a field at night.
Neighbours want to tie a tight rope, cut the wound and take him to a local healer.
His daughter Pallavi, a nursing student, says: ‘No cutting, no sucking, no healer. Keep his leg still and get him to the government hospital now.’
At the hospital he receives antivenom in time. The doctor says the hours saved made the difference.

steps.title: Snakebite in India: the facts
steps.body: India has among the highest numbers of snakebite deaths in the world — tens of thousands each year, mostly farmers, rural families and children. Most deaths are caused by the **‘Big Four’**: **Indian cobra, common krait, Russell’s viper and saw-scaled viper**. Many bites are from non-venomous snakes or are ‘dry’ bites, but you **can’t tell safely**, so treat every bite as an emergency. **Antivenom** is the only proven treatment and is available in many government hospitals.

steps.title: What to DO
steps.body:
1. Move away from the snake; don’t try to catch or kill it (a photo from a safe distance can help, but don’t waste time).
2. **Keep calm and still**; panic and movement can speed the spread of venom.
3. **Immobilise** the bitten limb like a fracture (splint, sling), keep it roughly at heart level.
4. Remove rings, bangles, anklets, watches and tight clothing (swelling comes fast).
5. **Go to the nearest hospital with antivenom immediately** — call 112 or 108; carry the person if possible rather than letting them walk.
6. Note the time of the bite and symptoms (drooping eyelids, difficulty breathing or swallowing, bleeding gums, swelling).

steps.title: What NOT to do (common myths)
steps.body:
- ❌ **Cutting** the wound or **sucking** out venom — causes infection and bleeding; doesn’t remove venom.
- ❌ **Tight tourniquets** or ropes — can cause severe tissue damage and loss of the limb.
- ❌ Ice, electric shock, chemicals, herbs, ‘snake stones’, alcohol.
- ❌ Waiting for a faith healer or ‘mantra’ treatment — the lost time is the most dangerous mistake.
- ❌ Assuming no pain means no danger: **krait bites** often happen at night to people sleeping on the floor and may be painless, yet deadly.
**Prevention**: sleep on a raised bed under a tucked-in mosquito net, carry a torch at night, wear boots in fields, clear rubbish and rat-attracting grain stores near homes.

steps.title: Dog and animal bites: rabies is preventable
steps.body:
Rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms start — but **completely preventable** with prompt care.
1. **Immediately wash the wound with soap and running water for about 15 minutes.**
2. Apply an antiseptic (such as povidone-iodine) if available.
3. **Go to a hospital the same day** for anti-rabies vaccine, and rabies immunoglobulin if the doctor advises (for deeper bites/scratches). Government hospitals provide these.
4. Complete **every dose** of the schedule.
This applies to bites or scratches from dogs, cats, monkeys and other mammals. Don’t apply chilli, turmeric or oil, and don’t wait to ‘watch the dog’ before starting treatment.

steps.title: Heat exhaustion and heatstroke
steps.body:
**Heat exhaustion**: heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea. Move to shade, loosen clothes, sip water or **ORS**, cool with wet cloths.
**Heatstroke** is an emergency: very high body temperature, confusion, slurred speech, fainting or fits, skin may be hot (dry or sweaty). **Call 112**, cool the person rapidly (water on skin, fan, wet sheets, ice packs at neck, armpits, groin), don’t give drinks if they are confused or unconscious.
Prevention in summer: drink water regularly, avoid strenuous work at midday, wear light loose cotton, cover the head, check on elderly neighbours and never leave children or pets in parked vehicles.

statements.why: It doesn’t remove venom and can cause infection.

statements.s: Antivenom given in a hospital is the proven treatment for venomous snakebite.
statements.why: Speed to hospital is the most important action.

statements.why: It’s the crucial first step, followed by vaccination.

statements.s: A tight rope above a snakebite is recommended.
statements.why: Tight tourniquets can cause limb damage and are not recommended.

statements.s: A confused, very hot person in summer may have heatstroke — a medical emergency.
statements.why: Call 112 and cool them rapidly.

quiz.why: Big Four: cobra, krait, Russell’s viper, saw-scaled viper.

quiz.why: Rehydrate gently with water/ORS.

lessons.title: Fire safety: prevent, escape, extinguish

scenes.text: At 2 am in a Mumbai apartment, 15-year-old Zubin wakes to a beeping smoke alarm and smells burning.
He touches the bedroom door with the back of his hand — it’s cool. He opens it slowly; smoke is near the ceiling.
He wakes his family; they crawl low, take the stairs (not the lift) and meet at the society gate.
They call 101 / 112. A short circuit in a neighbour’s flat had started the fire. Everyone escaped because they had practised.

steps.title: Prevention first
steps.body:
Most home fires start in the kitchen, from electrical faults, or from candles, diyas, mosquito coils, cigarettes and firecrackers.
- Never leave cooking unattended.
- Don’t overload sockets; replace damaged wires; switch off appliances at night.
- Keep diyas and candles away from curtains; don’t let children play with matches.
- Keep balconies and staircases free of clutter; never lock fire exits.
- Install **smoke alarms** and test them monthly.

steps.title: If there is a fire: get out, stay out, call
steps.body:
1. Shout ‘Fire!’ to warn everyone.
2. Before opening a door, feel it with the **back of your hand**. If hot, don’t open — use another way.
3. Smoke kills faster than flames: **crawl low** where air is cleaner; cover nose and mouth with cloth.
4. Use **stairs, never lifts**.
5. Close doors behind you to slow the fire.
6. Once out, **don’t go back in** for belongings.
7. Call **101** (fire) or **112**.
If trapped: close the door, block gaps with wet cloth, go to a window, signal with a cloth or torch, and call 112 with your exact location.

steps.title: Stop, drop and roll
steps.body: If your clothes catch fire: **Stop** (don’t run — running fans flames), **Drop** to the ground, cover your face with your hands, **Roll** over and over until flames are out. Then cool burns with water for 20 minutes. Help another person by wrapping them in a heavy blanket or rug (not synthetic) and rolling them.

steps.title: Using a fire extinguisher: PASS
steps.body:
Only for a **small fire** and only if you have a clear escape route behind you.
- **P**ull the pin.
- **A**im the nozzle at the **base** of the fire (not the flames).
- **S**queeze the handle.
- **S**weep side to side.
A common type is **ABC dry powder**, used on ordinary materials, flammable liquids and electrical fires (after switching power off if possible). **Never use water on electrical or oil fires.** If the fire doesn’t shrink within seconds, leave and call for help.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Draw your home’s escape plan: two ways out of each room, and a meeting point outside. Practise once with your family. Find your building’s extinguisher and check its pressure gauge is in the green.

lessons.title: Earthquakes: Drop, Cover, Hold On

scenes.text: Class 9 students in Guwahati are in maths class when the room begins to shake and the fan swings.
Their teacher, Mr. Bora, calls, ‘Drop, cover, hold on!’ Everyone gets under their desks, holding the legs.
The shaking lasts about 20 seconds. When it stops, they walk out calmly in a line to the open ground, away from buildings.
They wait for aftershocks to pass and for official updates. No one is hurt — they had drilled it twice that year.

steps.title: India’s earthquake risk
steps.body: A large part of India lies in moderate to very high seismic zones — especially the Himalayan belt, the North-East, parts of Gujarat (Kutch) and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands. Earthquakes can’t be predicted precisely, so **preparation** matters. Most injuries are caused by **falling objects and collapsing structures**, not the ground movement itself.

steps.title: During shaking: Drop, Cover, Hold On
steps.body:
- **Drop** onto your hands and knees before the shaking knocks you down.
- **Cover** your head and neck under a sturdy table or desk; if none, crouch next to an interior wall away from windows and cover your head with your arms.
- **Hold on** to your shelter until the shaking stops.
**Indoors**: stay in — don’t run out during shaking (falling debris near exits is deadly); avoid windows, glass, almirahs, hanging objects. Don’t use lifts.
**Outdoors**: move to an open area away from buildings, trees, poles and wires.
**In a vehicle**: stop in an open place, away from bridges and flyovers; stay inside.

steps.title: After the shaking
steps.body:
- Expect **aftershocks**; move carefully to open ground.
- Check yourself and others for injuries; give first aid.
- If you smell gas, don’t use flames or switches; turn off the regulator; leave.
- Avoid damaged buildings; listen to official updates on radio/TV/government apps.
- **If trapped**: cover your mouth with cloth, don’t light a match, tap on a pipe or wall or use a whistle so rescuers can hear; shout only as a last resort (to save energy and avoid inhaling dust).
- Use SMS or messages rather than calls to keep networks free.

steps.title: Prepare your home
steps.body:
- Fix heavy almirahs, bookshelves and water heaters to walls.
- Keep heavy items on low shelves; don’t hang heavy frames over beds.
- Know how to switch off gas and electricity.
- When building or buying, ask whether the structure follows earthquake-resistant codes (BIS codes for seismic design).

steps.title: Myths
steps.body:
- ‘Stand in a doorway’ — in modern homes doorways are not stronger than other parts, and doors swing; Drop, Cover, Hold On is safer.
- ‘Run outside immediately’ — many injuries happen to people running out while debris falls.
- Viral messages predicting the ‘exact date of the next big quake’ are false; earthquakes can’t be predicted that way.

lessons.title: Floods and cyclones

scenes.text: In Kerala’s monsoon, the Joseph family hears a district alert on TV: heavy rain, rivers may overflow.
Anna, 16, packs the emergency bag, puts documents in a waterproof pouch and charges power banks.
Her father wants to drive across a flooded road to reach relatives. Anna reminds him: ‘Just 30 cm of moving water can float a car.’
They go to the relief camp at the school on higher ground instead. Their house floods, but everyone is safe.

steps.title: Understand warnings
steps.body: The **India Meteorological Department (IMD)** issues colour-coded weather warnings: **Green** (no action), **Yellow** (be aware), **Orange** (be prepared), **Red** (take action). State and district disaster management authorities announce evacuations. Follow official channels — TV, radio, official government apps and SMS alerts — and ignore unverified forwards.

steps.title: Before and during a flood
steps.body:
**Before**: move valuables and documents up high; keep the emergency kit ready; know the nearest high ground or relief shelter; switch off the electricity main if water may enter.
**During**:
- **Never walk, swim or drive through flood water.** About 15 cm of fast water can knock an adult down, and around 30 cm can float many cars.
- Stay away from electric poles and fallen wires.
- If trapped in a building, go to the highest floor or roof (not a closed attic), signal for help.
- Drink only boiled, bottled or chlorinated water.

steps.title: Cyclones
steps.body: India’s east coast (Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu) and west coast (Gujarat, Maharashtra) face cyclones. **Before landfall**: follow evacuation orders, secure loose items, stock water and food, charge phones, store documents safely. **During**: stay indoors away from windows. The **‘eye’** may bring a sudden calm — **don’t go out**; winds return from the other direction. **After**: avoid fallen wires and damaged structures; wait for the official all-clear. Odisha’s strong early warning and evacuation system has greatly reduced cyclone deaths compared with the 1999 super cyclone — preparation works.

steps.title: After the water goes down
steps.body:
- Don’t switch on electricity until checked by an electrician.
- Watch for snakes and insects in homes.
- Throw away food that touched flood water.
- Disinfect water and surfaces; watch for diarrhoea, fever, leptospirosis (rat urine in flood water — seek a doctor if fever follows wading), dengue and malaria.
- Photograph damage for insurance and government relief claims.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Find the nearest relief shelter or high ground for your home. Save your district disaster control room number. Identify the weather-alert source you’ll trust.

lessons.title: Emergency kit and family plan

scenes.text: In Dehradun, Kamla keeps a backpack by the door labelled ‘Go bag’. Her son Arush thinks it’s silly.
One night, a landslide alert asks their colony to evacuate in 20 minutes.
While neighbours search for torches and medicines, Kamla and Arush grab the bag, documents and grandma’s pills and leave in five minutes.
The family meets at the agreed spot and informs an uncle in Delhi, their out-of-town contact.

steps.title: What goes in a go-bag
steps.body:
- Drinking water and dry food (biscuits, chana, dry fruits) for 2–3 days
- Torch, spare batteries, power bank, whistle
- First-aid kit and **regular medicines** (with a prescription copy)
- Copies of documents (Aadhaar, insurance, bank details) in a waterproof pouch; digital copies in DigiLocker
- Some cash in small notes
- A change of clothes, raincoat, blanket, face masks, sanitary pads, baby items if needed
- List of important phone numbers on paper (phones die)

steps.title: A family emergency plan
steps.body:
1. **Meeting points**: one near home, one outside the neighbourhood.
2. **Out-of-town contact**: one relative everyone informs (local networks often jam).
3. **Who helps whom**: elderly, children, people with disabilities, pets.
4. **Know how to shut off** gas, electricity and water.
5. **School/office plans**: know their evacuation procedures.
6. **Practise** twice a year; update the bag (expiry dates) every six months.

steps.title: Important numbers
steps.body:
- **112**: all emergencies
- **101**: fire · **108**: ambulance in many states · **102**: ambulance/maternal in many states
- **1070** (state) / **1077** (district): disaster helplines in many states
- **1098**: Childline (children in need)
- **1930**: cyber fraud
- **14416**: Tele-MANAS mental health support
Save them in your phone and on paper.

steps.title: Don’t forget mind and community
steps.body: Disasters are frightening, especially for children. Explain plans calmly, give children small tasks, and check on neighbours who live alone. After a disaster, sleep problems and fear are common — talk about it, keep routines, and seek help (Tele-MANAS 14416) if distress continues.

lessons.title: Helmets, seatbelts and speed

scenes.text: Varun, 17, rides pillion with his cousin to a shop two kilometres away in Patna. ‘No helmet, it’s just a short ride.’
A cow steps onto the road; the scooter skids. Varun’s head hits the kerb.
He survives with a serious head injury and months of recovery. His cousin, who wore a strapped helmet, has only bruises.
Varun now tells his school friends: ‘Most crashes happen close to home. Strap it, every time.’

steps.title: Why this matters
steps.body: Road crashes kill well over a lakh people in India every year, and a large share are young people and two-wheeler riders. Most crashes are preventable. Four big killers: **speeding, not wearing helmets, not wearing seatbelts, and drunk or distracted driving**.

steps.title: Helmets: wear it right
steps.body: Under the Motor Vehicles Act, helmets are compulsory for riders **and pillion riders** on two-wheelers (with limited exemptions such as for turban-wearing Sikhs). Choose a **BIS-certified (ISI-marked)** helmet that fits snugly, and **fasten the chin strap** — an unstrapped helmet flies off in a crash. Replace a helmet after any serious impact. Children on two-wheelers also need proper protection.

steps.title: Seatbelts and child seats
steps.body: Seatbelts are required for front **and rear** seats. In a crash, an unbelted rear passenger can be thrown forward with great force and injure themselves and those in front. Airbags work **with** seatbelts, not instead. Children should ride in the **back seat** in an age-appropriate child restraint; never hold a baby on your lap in a car.

steps.title: Speed and stopping distance
steps.body:
Stopping distance = **reaction distance** + **braking distance**. In about 1 second of reaction time:
- At 36 km/h you travel 10 m before even braking.
- At 72 km/h you travel 20 m — and braking distance roughly **quadruples** when speed doubles.
So a small speed increase makes a big difference in crash force and stopping. Slow down near schools, markets, curves, at night, and in rain or fog.

steps.title: Underage driving
steps.body: In India, you can get a learner’s licence for a gearless two-wheeler up to 50 cc at **16** (with parent/guardian consent), and for other vehicles at **18**. Driving without a licence is illegal and dangerous; the Motor Vehicles Act provides strict penalties when a juvenile commits an offence, including for the guardian or owner of the vehicle.

statements.s: Pillion riders on two-wheelers must also wear helmets.
statements.why: The law and physics apply to both.

statements.s: An unstrapped helmet protects just as well.
statements.why: It can come off before impact.

statements.s: Rear-seat passengers in cars need seatbelts too.
statements.why: Unbelted rear passengers are thrown forward in crashes.

statements.s: Airbags make seatbelts unnecessary.
statements.why: Airbags are designed to work with seatbelts.

statements.s: Doubling speed roughly quadruples braking distance.
statements.why: Braking distance grows with the square of speed.

quiz.q: A good helmet in India should be…
quiz.why: Certified and properly fastened.

quiz.q: Where should young children sit in a car?
options: On an adult’s lap in front
In the back seat in a suitable child restraint
quiz.why: Back seat with restraint is safest.

quiz.q: At 72 km/h, distance travelled in 1 second is about…
Minimum age to get a learner’s licence for most motor vehicles (non-gearless ≤50cc) in India?
quiz.why: 18; 16 only for gearless up to 50 cc with consent.
