lessons.title: Passwords that are strong and memorable

scenes.text: Aarav, 15, in Lucknow uses ‘Aarav@2010’ for his game account, email and Instagram.
A gaming site he once joined is hacked and its password list leaks online.
Within days, someone logs into his email and Instagram using the same password and starts messaging his friends for money.
His sister Mahi helps him reset everything with different long passphrases saved in a password manager.

steps.title: How passwords get stolen
steps.body:
- **Data breaches**: a website is hacked and its password list leaks. Attackers then try the same email + password on other sites (**credential stuffing**).
- **Guessing**: computers can try billions of combinations; short or common passwords (123456, name+birth year, ‘password’) fall in seconds.
- **Phishing**: fake login pages trick you into typing your password.
- **Shoulder surfing** or sharing with friends.

steps.title: Length beats complexity: the passphrase
steps.body:
A **passphrase** is several random words joined together, for example: **‘mango-river-bicycle-cloud-47’**. It is long (hard for computers), and easy to picture (easy for you).
- Use at least **4–5 random words** or **14+ characters**.
- Avoid song lyrics, famous quotes, names, birthdays, pet names, phone numbers.
- **‘P@ssw0rd!’** looks complex but is in every hacker’s list.

steps.title: One account, one password
steps.body:
Reusing a password means one breach unlocks everything. The most important accounts — **email** (it resets all others), **banking/UPI** and **phone/cloud account** — must have unique, strong passwords.
A **password manager** (a reputable app, or the one built into your phone or browser) creates and remembers a unique password for every site; you remember just one strong master passphrase. Some services let you check whether your email appeared in known breaches.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing passwords on a sticky note on the laptop.
- Saving passwords in a plain notes app or WhatsApp chat to yourself.
- Sharing passwords with a best friend or partner (relationships change).
- Logging in on shared/cyber-café computers and forgetting to log out.
- Changing ‘Password1’ to ‘Password2’.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Pick your email account. Create a new passphrase of 5 random words (open a book to random pages for words if you like), change it now, and turn on 2FA (next lesson).

activity.prompt: Strong or weak password?

items.text: A unique 20-character password made by a password manager

quiz.q: Which makes a password hardest to crack?
quiz.why: Length increases combinations enormously.

quiz.q: Why is reusing passwords dangerous?
options: One breach unlocks all your accounts
quiz.why: Attackers try leaked passwords everywhere.

quiz.q: Which account needs the strongest unique password first?
quiz.why: Email can reset all other passwords.

quiz.q: A password manager…
options: Stores passwords in plain text for anyone
Creates and remembers unique passwords behind one master passphrase
quiz.why: It removes the need to reuse passwords.

lessons.title: Two-factor authentication, OTPs and passkeys

scenes.text: Mrs. Fernandes, 64, in Goa gets a call: ‘Ma’am, I’m from your bank. To stop your card being blocked, read me the OTP we just sent.’
The SMS says: ‘OTP for transaction of ₹49,999… Do not share with anyone, including bank staff.’
She remembers her grandson’s rule: ‘An OTP is like a house key. Nobody genuine ever asks for it.’ She hangs up.
She calls the bank’s number from the back of her card. Her account was never at risk — the caller was a fraudster.

steps.title: What 2FA is
steps.body:
**Two-factor authentication (2FA)** — also called multi-factor (MFA) or two-step verification — asks for two different kinds of proof:
- **Something you know**: password or PIN
- **Something you have**: phone, OTP, security key
- **Something you are**: fingerprint, face
Even if a criminal steals your password, they can’t log in without the second factor. Turning on 2FA for email, social media, cloud and banking blocks most account takeovers.

steps.title: Types of second factor (weakest to strongest)
steps.body:
- **SMS OTP**: much better than nothing, but vulnerable to SIM-swap fraud and to people tricking you into sharing it.
- **Authenticator app** (time-based codes that change every 30 seconds): stronger; works without network.
- **Push approval** in an app: convenient, but never approve a login you didn’t start (‘MFA fatigue’ attacks spam you with prompts).
- **Passkeys and hardware security keys**: strongest; they resist phishing because they only work on the real website. Many big services now support passkeys that use your phone’s fingerprint or face unlock.

steps.title: The OTP rule
steps.body: **An OTP is only for you to type into a website or app you opened yourself.** No bank, police, courier, telecom company, delivery person or ‘customer care’ will ever need it. If someone asks for an OTP, it’s a scam — 100% of the time. Also read OTP messages fully: they often say what the OTP will authorise (a payment, a login, a SIM change).

steps.title: Backup codes
steps.body: When you turn on 2FA, services usually give **backup/recovery codes**. Print or write them and keep them somewhere safe (not in the same phone). If you lose your phone, these let you back in. Also keep your recovery email and phone number up to date.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Open your email account’s security settings. Turn on 2-step verification, add an authenticator app or passkey if possible, and save backup codes on paper.

statements.s: A bank employee may ask for your OTP to stop your card being blocked.
statements.why: Banks never ask for OTPs. It is always a scam.

statements.s: With 2FA on, a stolen password alone is usually not enough to log in.
statements.why: The second factor stops the attacker.

statements.s: Authenticator apps are generally safer than SMS OTPs.
statements.why: They are not exposed to SIM-swap and SMS interception.

statements.s: If you get a login approval prompt you didn’t start, you should approve it to make it stop.
statements.why: Deny it and change your password — someone has it.

statements.s: Backup codes should be stored somewhere other than your phone.
statements.why: So you can recover if the phone is lost.

quiz.q: Which is ‘something you have’?
quiz.why: Possession factor.

quiz.q: Who can you share an OTP with?
options: Nobody — only type it into a site/app you opened
quiz.why: OTPs are never needed by anyone else.

quiz.q: Which second factor resists phishing best?
quiz.why: Passkeys only work on the genuine site.

quiz.q: You get 10 login approval prompts at midnight. You should…
options: Deny all, change password, check account activity
quiz.why: Someone has your password and is trying to push in.

lessons.title: Securing your phone and laptop

scenes.text: Ritu, 20, in Indore downloads a ‘free movies’ APK file shared on a Telegram group.
It asks for permission to read SMS, access contacts and ‘display over other apps’. She taps Allow on everything.
Two days later, ₹12,000 is withdrawn using OTPs she never saw — the app was reading her SMS.
Her friend Danish shows her how to remove the app, check permissions and keep updates on. She reports the fraud at 1930 quickly.

steps.title: Five basic protections
steps.body:
1. **Updates**: install system and app updates promptly; they fix security holes.
2. **Screen lock**: PIN (6+ digits) or passphrase plus fingerprint/face. Avoid simple patterns.
3. **Official app stores only**: don’t install APK files from links, WhatsApp or Telegram; check developer name, reviews and downloads.
4. **Permissions**: give only what makes sense — a torch app doesn’t need contacts or SMS. Review permissions every few months.
5. **Find my device**: turn it on so you can locate, lock or erase a lost phone.

steps.title: Dangerous permissions to question
steps.body:
- **SMS** access (can read OTPs)
- **Accessibility** service (can see and tap on your screen)
- **Display over other apps** (can place fake screens over banking apps)
- **Device admin** (hard to uninstall)
- **Screen-sharing / remote-access** apps installed on a stranger’s instruction
If an app you don’t trust has these, uninstall it and change banking/email passwords from a safe device.

steps.title: Backups: the 3-2-1 idea
steps.body: Keep **3 copies** of important data (photos, documents), on **2 different types** of storage (phone + laptop/external drive), with **1 copy off-site** (cloud backup). If your phone is stolen, dropped in water or hit by ransomware, you lose nothing important.

steps.title: Public Wi-Fi and SIM safety
steps.body:
- On public Wi-Fi, avoid banking; use mobile data or a trusted VPN. Websites with HTTPS encrypt traffic, but fake hotspots exist.
- Set a **SIM PIN** so a stolen SIM can’t be used in another phone.
- If your phone suddenly loses network for a long time without reason and you get alerts about SIM change, contact your telecom provider immediately — it could be a **SIM-swap** attempt.
- The government’s **Sanchar Saathi** portal lets you check mobile connections registered in your name and request blocking of a lost/stolen phone.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Go to Settings → Apps → Permissions on your phone. Find which apps can read SMS and which have accessibility access. Remove any that don’t need it.

activity.prompt: Phone security check-up
items: System updated to the latest version
Screen lock set (6+ digit PIN or passphrase)
No apps installed from unknown links
Checked connections in my name on Sanchar Saathi

quiz.q: Why install updates promptly?
options: They fix security holes attackers use
quiz.why: Updates patch known vulnerabilities.

quiz.q: A torch app asks for SMS access. You…
quiz.why: A torch doesn’t need SMS; this suggests malware.

quiz.q: The 3-2-1 backup rule means…
quiz.why: Redundancy protects against loss.

quiz.q: Which government portal helps check mobile connections in your name and block lost phones?
quiz.why: Sanchar Saathi is run by the Department of Telecommunications.

lessons.title: Hacked or lost phone: the recovery plan

scenes.text: Kunal, 19, a dance creator in Delhi with 20,000 followers, gets an email saying his account email was changed.
Minutes later, his account posts crypto ads and DMs his followers asking for money.
His friend Sara, who works in IT, walks him through a calm recovery: secure email first, use the platform’s official recovery, warn followers from another account.
In two days he has the account back, with 2FA and a passkey. He now checks ‘where you’re logged in’ monthly.

steps.title: Signs you may be hacked
steps.body:
- Emails about password or email changes you didn’t make
- Friends receive messages you didn’t send
- Unknown logins, devices or locations in security settings
- Unknown transactions
- Phone suddenly slow, hot, full of pop-ups, or new apps you didn’t install

steps.title: Step-by-step recovery
steps.body:
1. **From a clean device**, change the password of your **email first**, then the affected account.
2. Use **official recovery** pages only (not DMs offering ‘recovery services’ — those are scams).
3. **Sign out of all sessions/devices** in security settings.
4. Check and fix **recovery email/phone**, and remove unknown linked apps.
5. **Turn on 2FA** (authenticator or passkey).
6. **Warn contacts** that messages from you may be fake.
7. If money is involved: call **1930** and your bank immediately; report at **cybercrime.gov.in**.
8. Scan/clean your device; if it’s badly infected, back up data and factory reset.

steps.title: Lost or stolen phone
steps.body:
1. Use **find my device** to locate, lock or erase it.
2. Call your telecom provider to **block the SIM** and get a replacement SIM.
3. Ask your bank to block UPI/mobile banking if the phone was unlocked or you fear misuse.
4. File a police complaint (many states allow online lost-property reports).
5. Use **Sanchar Saathi (CEIR)** to request blocking of the phone’s IMEI so it can’t be used on Indian networks; it can be unblocked if recovered.
6. Change passwords of email and important apps.

steps.title: Avoid second scams
steps.body: After a hack, fake ‘recovery experts’ and ‘cyber police’ often contact victims promising to get money or accounts back for a fee. Genuine police don’t charge fees and official platforms don’t recover accounts through DMs. Report only through official portals and helplines.

steps.title: Prepare before it happens
steps.body: Keep backup codes on paper, know your IMEI (dial *#06#) and write it down, keep recovery email and phone updated, and save 1930 in your contacts.

a.text: You get an alert: ‘Your email recovery phone number was changed.’ You didn’t do it.

choices.label: Ignore it — probably a glitch
choices.feedback: Changes to recovery details are a classic first step in takeovers.

choices.label: Immediately log in from a trusted device, change password, restore your number, sign out other sessions
choices.feedback: Fast action stops the attacker.

b.text: You’re back in. A DM arrives: ‘I’m a certified hacker, I can secure your accounts for ₹2,000.’

choices.label: Pay — they sound professional
choices.feedback: These ‘recovery’ offers are scams.

choices.label: Ignore and block; turn on 2FA and check linked apps
choices.feedback: Correct.

bad.text: The attacker or scammer gains more control. Use official recovery pages, report at cybercrime.gov.in, and call 1930 if money is involved.

good.text: Account secured with 2FA. You also warned your contacts. Well handled.

quiz.q: Which account should you secure first after a hack?
quiz.why: Email can reset all others.

quiz.q: How do you find your phone’s IMEI?
quiz.why: *#06# displays the IMEI.

quiz.q: A DM offers paid ‘account recovery’. This is…
quiz.why: Recover only through official channels.

quiz.q: After money is stolen through a hacked account, call…
quiz.why: Quick reports help freeze funds.

questions.q: Which is the strongest password?
Should you share an OTP with a bank official on the phone?
Install apps from…
2FA protects because…
options: It needs a second proof beyond the password

questions.q: Credential stuffing is…
options: Trying leaked passwords on other sites

questions.q: Which permission is most dangerous for an unknown app?
questions.why: It can read and control your screen.

questions.q: A phone loses network unexpectedly for hours and you get a SIM-change alert. Likely risk?
3-2-1 backup means 1 copy is…
questions.why: Off-site protects against theft or disaster.

questions.q: Which is the best order after a hack?
options: Post about it, then change password
Secure email → change affected password → sign out all sessions → enable 2FA → warn contacts

questions.q: Why are passkeys phishing-resistant?
options: They are bound to the genuine website and can’t be typed into a fake page
questions.why: Cryptographic keys work only with the real domain.

questions.q: ‘MFA fatigue’ attack means…
options: Spamming approval prompts hoping you tap Approve
questions.why: Never approve prompts you didn’t start.

questions.q: Phone stolen, unlocked, UPI app on it. Most urgent pair of actions?
options: Block SIM with telecom and block UPI/mobile banking with bank; then IMEI block via CEIR and police report
questions.why: Cut access to money and OTPs first.

questions.q: Which setup gives the best protection for a primary email account?
options: Unique long passphrase in a password manager + passkey/authenticator 2FA + backup codes on paper
Same password as bank for easy memory

courses.title: Scams, digital arrest, deepfakes & sextortion
courses.summary: How scammers hook people, India’s most common frauds (digital arrest, parcel, task/job, KYC), how to check deepfakes and voice clones, and what to do about online blackmail.
outcomes: Learners can name the psychological triggers scams use
Learners can recognise digital arrest, parcel, task and KYC frauds
Learners can verify a suspicious call or video using a second channel and a family code word
Learners know sextortion is never the victim’s fault and exactly how to report it
Learners can report fraud through 1930, cybercrime.gov.in and Chakshu
courses.guardianNote: Lesson 4 explains online blackmail (sextortion) in calm, non-explicit language: what it is, that it is never the victim’s fault, not to pay, how to keep evidence and where to report (1930, cybercrime.gov.in, 1098 for under-18s). No images or explicit descriptions. Teenagers are frequent targets, so knowing this protects them.

lessons.title: How scams hook you: the four triggers

scenes.text: Gopal, 58, a shopkeeper in Varanasi, gets an SMS: ‘Congratulations! You won ₹25 lakh in a lucky draw. Pay ₹4,999 processing fee.’
A ‘manager’ calls: ‘Pay within 2 hours or the prize goes to the next winner.’
His granddaughter Diya asks: ‘Dadaji, did you buy a ticket?’ He hadn’t.
They report the number via the Chakshu facility on Sanchar Saathi. Gopal now pauses before any ‘urgent’ money request.

steps.title: Scams work on emotions, not intelligence
steps.body:
Clever, educated people are scammed every day. Scammers use four triggers:
- **Urgency**: ‘in 30 minutes’, ‘today only’.
- **Authority**: pretending to be police, bank, CBI, courier, telecom, your boss.
- **Fear**: arrest, account block, power cut, a relative in trouble.
- **Greed or hope**: prize, job, high returns, cashback, romance.
When you feel a strong emotion plus pressure to act fast, that is your signal to **stop**.

steps.title: Spotting phishing links and messages
steps.body:
- Check the **sender**: banks use official short codes; random mobile numbers are a warning.
- Look carefully at **web addresses**: ‘sbi-kyc-update.xyz’ is not your bank. Look for misspellings and extra words.
- **Shortened links** hide destinations.
- Grammar errors, generic greetings (‘Dear customer’).
- Requests for OTP, PIN, CVV, passwords, remote-access apps or payment to ‘unlock’ something.
- Unexpected attachments (especially .apk files).

steps.title: The STOP–CHECK–CALL rule
steps.body:
1. **STOP**: don’t click, pay or share anything right now.
2. **CHECK**: search the official website/app yourself; ask a family member.
3. **CALL**: contact the organisation using the number from its official site, app or the back of your card — never the number in the message.
Genuine organisations will still be there in 10 minutes.

steps.title: Where to report
steps.body:
- **1930**: National Cyber Crime Helpline (financial fraud — call fast)
- **cybercrime.gov.in**: National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal
- **Chakshu** on the Sanchar Saathi portal: report suspected fraud calls, SMS and WhatsApp messages (even if you didn’t lose money)
- Your bank’s official helpline for blocking cards/UPI

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Open your SMS inbox. Find one message that might be a scam. List which of the four triggers it uses and what clues give it away.

activity.prompt: Likely scam or likely genuine?

items.text: ‘Your KYC expires today. Click bit.ly/xyz to update or account blocked.’
Bank app notification of a payment you just made
‘You won a car! Pay ₹9,999 GST to claim.’
OTP SMS that arrives right after you log in to your own bank app
‘Electricity will be cut tonight. Call this mobile number now.’
‘Part-time job: like YouTube videos, earn ₹5,000 daily.’

quiz.q: Which is NOT a common scam trigger?
options: Patient explanation with time to verify
quiz.why: Scammers rush you; genuine bodies give time.

quiz.q: To verify a bank message, call…
options: The number on the bank’s official site/app or back of card
quiz.why: Use independently found official contacts.

quiz.q: Chakshu on Sanchar Saathi is for…
quiz.why: It lets citizens report suspected fraud communications.

quiz.q: Why are educated people also scammed?
options: Scams target emotions and pressure, not intelligence
quiz.why: Anyone can be rushed into a mistake.

sources: I4C — National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

lessons.title: India’s top frauds: digital arrest, parcels, tasks and KYC

story.title: Six hours on a video call

scenes.text: Dr. Menon, a retired professor in Thiruvananthapuram, gets a call: ‘A parcel in your name with illegal drugs has been seized. Connecting you to the police.’
On a video call, a man in police uniform with an official-looking background says he is under ‘digital arrest’ and must not tell anyone.
He is told to transfer his savings to a ‘RBI verification account’ to prove innocence.
His daughter Leena walks in, sees the screen, ends the call and phones 1930. There is no such thing as a digital arrest.

steps.title: ‘Digital arrest’ is a scam — always
steps.body: **There is no ‘digital arrest’ in Indian law.** Police, CBI, ED, customs, RBI or courts do **not** arrest people over video calls, keep them on camera for hours, or ask them to transfer money to ‘verify’ or ‘safe’ accounts. Real legal processes involve written notices and in-person procedures. If anyone says you’re under digital arrest: **hang up, don’t pay, tell family, call 1930**. The government has run national awareness campaigns about this exact fraud.

steps.title: Other common frauds
steps.body:
- **Parcel/courier**: ‘Your parcel has drugs/passports’ — leads to digital-arrest style threats.
- **Task/job scam**: paid to like videos or rate hotels; small payouts first, then ‘pay to unlock bigger tasks’ — money vanishes.
- **KYC/account-block**: link or app to ‘update KYC’ steals banking details.
- **Fake customer care** numbers on search results.
- **‘Hi Mum/Dad, new number’**: a ‘child’ texts from an unknown number asking urgently for money.
- **Investment groups** promising high guaranteed returns.
- **Marketplace buyer/seller** (QR code to ‘receive’ money).
- **Sextortion** (covered in lesson 4).

steps.title: Why task scams feel real
steps.body: Day 1: you like 3 videos, get ₹150. Day 2: ₹300. Day 3: ‘Prepaid task: invest ₹1,000, get ₹1,300.’ It pays. Day 4: ‘Invest ₹10,000 for ₹14,000.’ Your dashboard shows profit, but withdrawal is ‘blocked until you complete the next task of ₹50,000’. The early small payouts were bait. **Any job that asks you to pay to earn is a scam.**

steps.title: Protect elders and family
steps.body: Talk to parents and grandparents about digital arrest and parcel scams — fraudsters target retired people with savings. Agree a rule: **‘No money transfer to anyone new, for any reason, without calling a family member first.’** Help them set transaction limits.

steps.title: Around the world
steps.body: Similar tricks exist everywhere: fake tax-office calls in the USA and UK, ‘police impersonation’ scams in China, ‘parcel stuck at customs’ texts in Europe. The pattern — authority + fear + secrecy + money transfer — is universal.

a.text: A caller says: ‘This is the cyber crime branch. Your Aadhaar is linked to money laundering. Stay on this video call; you are under digital arrest. Tell no one.’

choices.label: Stay on the call and follow instructions
choices.feedback: This is exactly how the scam works — isolation and fear.

choices.label: Hang up, tell a family member and call 1930
choices.feedback: Perfect. Digital arrest does not exist.

b.text: They show a fake arrest warrant with logos and ask you to transfer ₹3 lakh to a ‘secret supervision account’ to clear your name.

choices.label: Transfer the money
choices.feedback: The money goes straight to criminals.

choices.label: End the call now and report it
choices.feedback: It’s never too late to hang up.

bad.text: Call 1930 immediately and your bank; report on cybercrime.gov.in with all details. Speed can help freeze money.

good.text: You’re safe. Real police never arrest by video call or ask for money transfers.

quiz.q: ‘Digital arrest’ over video call is…
quiz.why: No such procedure exists in Indian law.

quiz.q: A job asks you to pay ₹2,000 to ‘unlock’ higher-paying tasks. It is…
quiz.why: Real jobs don’t ask you to pay to earn.

quiz.q: A ‘new number’ message from your ‘son’ asks for urgent money. Best action?
options: Call your son on his old known number to verify
quiz.why: Verify through a known channel.

quiz.q: Which do scammers often demand to keep you trapped?
options: That you visit a police station
quiz.why: Isolation prevents you from getting advice.

sources: Ministry of Home Affairs public awareness campaigns

lessons.title: Deepfakes and voice clones: seeing is no longer believing

scenes.text: Simran, 21, in Chandigarh gets a call. It’s her father’s voice, crying: ‘Beta, I’ve had an accident, send ₹50,000 to this number, quickly!’
Something feels off — he calls her ‘beta’ but never says their family nickname.
She asks: ‘What’s our code word?’ The line goes silent and disconnects.
She calls her father’s own number — he’s safe at his office. The voice was cloned from his public videos.

steps.title: What deepfakes are
steps.body:
**Deepfakes** are fake videos, images or audio made with AI so that someone appears to say or do things they never did. **Voice cloning** can copy a voice from a few seconds of recording (from reels, voice notes or videos). They are used for:
- Fake emergency calls from ‘family’
- Fake celebrity or CEO videos promoting investments or apps
- Fake ‘boss’ calls asking staff to transfer money
- Harassment and fake intimate images
- Political misinformation

steps.title: Clues — but don’t rely on them alone
steps.body: Some deepfakes show odd blinking, blurry edges around face or hair, mismatched lip-sync, strange lighting, robotic tone or unnatural pauses. But the technology is improving quickly, so **don’t trust your eyes and ears alone**. The reliable defence is **verification through another channel**.

steps.title: Your verification toolkit
steps.body:
1. **Family code word**: agree a secret word or question with family that’s never posted online.
2. **Call back** on the number you already have saved — not the number calling you.
3. **Ask a personal question** only the real person would know.
4. **Slow down**: urgency + money = verify first.
5. For workplaces: any payment request by call/video must be confirmed through a second official channel.
6. For viral videos: check whether trusted news outlets or official accounts report the same thing; government claims can be checked with **PIB Fact Check**.

steps.title: Fake images of real people
steps.body: Creating or sharing fake intimate or defamatory images of a person without consent causes serious harm and can be a crime in India (for example under the IT Act provisions on privacy violation and cheating by personation, and under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita). Platforms must remove such content when reported. If it happens to you: save evidence (links, screenshots), report to the platform, report at cybercrime.gov.in, and tell someone you trust. **It is not your fault.**

steps.title: Reduce your exposure
steps.body: Keep social accounts private where possible, limit long public voice clips, and think before posting children’s photos publicly. You can’t remove all risk, but you can make yourself a harder target.

items.front: A video of a famous cricketer promoting a ‘guaranteed returns’ trading app
items.back: Very likely a deepfake ad. Celebrities’ faces and voices are often faked for investment scams. Don’t install; report the ad.

items.front: Your ‘boss’ on a video call asks you to urgently transfer company funds and keep it secret
items.back: Verify through a separate official channel (call their known number, email your finance team). Secrecy + urgency = red flag.

items.front: A crying ‘relative’ calls from an unknown number asking for money
items.back: Ask the family code word and call the relative back on their saved number.

items.front: A viral clip shows a minister announcing free money for everyone
items.back: Check official sources and PIB Fact Check before sharing.

items.front: Someone sends you a fake intimate image of a classmate
items.back: Don’t forward it. Report to the platform and cybercrime.gov.in, and support the person harmed.

quiz.q: The most reliable way to check a suspicious ‘family emergency’ call is…
options: Call the person back on their known number / use a code word
quiz.why: Verification through a separate channel defeats clones.

quiz.q: Voice clones can be made from…
options: Short clips from social media or voice notes
quiz.why: Modern tools need very little audio.

quiz.q: Spotting visual glitches is…
options: Helpful but not reliable as deepfakes improve
quiz.why: Always verify through another channel.

quiz.q: You receive a fake intimate image of someone. You should…
options: Not share; report it and support the person
quiz.why: Sharing multiplies harm and may be a crime.

lessons.title: Online blackmail (sextortion): not your fault, don’t pay, get help

scenes.text: Nikhil, 17, in Nagpur chats with a friendly ‘girl’ on Instagram who soon asks to video call. Later he gets a threat: a recording, edited to look embarrassing.
‘Pay ₹10,000 in one hour or I send this to your family and school.’ He feels sick and alone and thinks his life is over.
He finally tells his older cousin Raj. Raj says, ‘This is a crime against you. You did nothing that deserves this. We’ll handle it together.’
They stop replying, save evidence, report the account, file a complaint at cybercrime.gov.in and call 1098. The threats stop.

steps.title: What sextortion is
steps.body: **Sextortion** is blackmail where someone threatens to share private or fake intimate images or videos unless the victim pays money, sends more images or does something else. Criminal gangs run it as a business, often with fake profiles. Teenagers and young men are frequent targets, but anyone can be. Images can be stolen, secretly recorded, or completely **fake (AI-made)**.

steps.title: The four rules
steps.body:
1. **It is not your fault.** The criminal is the one breaking the law.
2. **Don’t pay.** Paying usually leads to more demands, not deletion.
3. **Stop contact, but keep evidence**: screenshot chats, usernames, profile links, payment details. Don’t delete the account until evidence is saved; then block.
4. **Tell a trusted adult and report**: cybercrime.gov.in (it has a category for women- and child-related crimes), **1930**, or the local police. Under-18s and their families can call **Childline 1098**. Report the account on the platform.

steps.title: Getting images removed
steps.body:
- Report on the platform: major platforms remove non-consensual intimate content.
- **StopNCII.org** helps adults (18+) prevent intimate images from being shared on participating platforms by creating a digital fingerprint (‘hash’) — the image itself isn’t uploaded.
- **Take It Down** (run by NCMEC) does similar work for images taken when the person was under 18.
- Indian law treats creating or sharing sexual content involving anyone under 18 as a serious crime under the POCSO Act and the IT Act — that protects the child, who is the victim.

steps.title: If you’re feeling hopeless
steps.body: Blackmailers want you to feel there’s no way out. That feeling is temporary, and help works. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, tell someone now or call **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7) or **112** in an emergency. Families: respond with support, not anger — the child is the victim.

steps.title: Prevention
steps.body:
- Be cautious with new online contacts who quickly become flirty or push for private video calls.
- Keep accounts private; don’t accept requests from strangers.
- Remember that anything sent can be saved and shared.
- Agree with friends: ‘If anyone ever threatens you, tell me — no judgement.’

activity.prompt: Questions people are too scared to ask

items.q: If I pay once, will they delete it?
items.a: Almost never. Payment shows you can pay, so demands usually increase. Don’t pay; report instead.

items.q: Will I get in trouble with the police for what was in the image?
items.a: If you are a victim of blackmail, police and Childline are there to help you. The blackmailer is the offender. Talk to a trusted adult and report.

items.q: Should I delete my chats right away?
items.a: Save screenshots and links first — they are evidence. Then block and report.

items.q: What if the image is fake?
items.a: AI-made fakes are also a crime to create and share for harassment. The same steps apply: don’t pay, save evidence, report.

items.q: I’m too ashamed to tell my parents.
items.a: Many people feel that. Choose any trusted adult — a cousin, teacher, counsellor — or call 1098 (Childline) or 14416 (Tele-MANAS). You don’t have to handle this alone.

quiz.q: First rule if someone blackmails you online?
options: Don’t pay; save evidence; tell someone; report
quiz.why: Paying fuels more demands.

quiz.q: Whose fault is sextortion?
quiz.why: The criminal is responsible.

quiz.q: A child in India being blackmailed can call…
quiz.why: Childline supports children in distress.

quiz.q: StopNCII.org is for…
options: Adults’ intimate images, using a digital fingerprint
quiz.why: It helps prevent sharing without uploading the image itself.

sources: I4C — National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

questions.q: Which trigger is ‘Act in 30 minutes or lose your account’?
‘sbi-kyc-help.top’ is most likely…
A family code word helps against…

options: Pay small amounts first, then ask you to invest larger sums

questions.why: Chakshu accepts reports of suspected fraud communications.

questions.q: Why shouldn’t you rely only on visual glitches to detect deepfakes?
options: Deepfakes are improving and may show no glitches

questions.q: Which tool helps under-18s remove intimate images taken when they were minors?
questions.why: Run by NCMEC for images of minors.

options: Video-call arrest, secrecy demand and money transfer to ‘verify’ — none are real procedures

questions.q: Your company CFO appears on video asking you to wire ₹40 lakh urgently and confidentially. Best response?
options: Follow the company’s verification process via a separate known channel before any transfer
questions.why: Deepfake CEO/CFO fraud is real; out-of-band verification stops it.

options: Reassure it’s not their fault, don’t pay, save evidence, report (cybercrime.gov.in/1930/1098), and connect to support such as Tele-MANAS 14416
Confiscate the phone and ignore it
questions.why: Safety, support and reporting together protect the child.

options: Only uneducated people fall for them
They exploit emotions and pressure; verification habits protect everyone

lessons.title: Your digital footprint and privacy settings

scenes.text: Tanvi, 16, from Kochi posts an excited photo of her boarding pass: ‘Off to Singapore!’
A stranger uses the code on the pass to view and try to change her booking. Another notices from her stories that her home is empty.
Her old posts also show her school uniform and the route she walks every day.
Her aunt, a cybersecurity analyst, helps her clean up: private account, location off, and a new rule — post memories after, not during, trips.

steps.title: Your footprint lasts
steps.body: Your **digital footprint** is everything about you online: posts, comments, likes, photos, tags, and data apps collect. Deleting a post doesn’t delete screenshots others took. Colleges, employers and future partners may search your name. Ask before posting: **Would I be OK with my grandmother, a teacher and a stranger seeing this in five years?**

steps.title: Never post these publicly
steps.body:
- Aadhaar, PAN, passport or card photos (even partly)
- Boarding passes and tickets (barcodes contain booking details)
- Your exact home address, school uniform with name, daily routes
- Live location while you’re out (‘at the mall now’) or ‘house empty’ posts
- OTPs, bank screenshots, QR codes
- Photos of other people (especially children) without permission

steps.title: A 10-minute privacy check-up
steps.body:
1. Set accounts to **private**; review followers — remove strangers.
2. Turn off **location tagging** and remove location from photos.
3. Control **who can tag you, message you and see your friends list**.
4. Check **app permissions** (location, contacts, microphone).
5. Remove old apps and accounts you no longer use.
6. Search your own name and see what appears.
7. Use masked Aadhaar (shows only the last 4 digits) when a copy is needed.

steps.title: Your data rights in India
steps.body: The **Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023** sets rules for how organisations collect and use personal data. It is built around **consent** for specific purposes and gives individuals rights such as accessing information about their data, correction and erasure, and grievance redressal. For children’s data, organisations need verifiable parental consent. Its rules are being brought into force in phases, so check the current status.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Do the 10-minute check-up on your most-used app now. Then scroll your own profile as if you were a stranger: what could you learn?

activity.prompt: Safe to share publicly, or think twice?

items.text: ‘Whole family away for a week!’ while travelling
Your school name and daily bus stop
Holiday photos posted after you return

quiz.q: Why avoid posting boarding passes?
options: Barcodes contain booking details that can be misused
quiz.why: Booking codes can allow access to your reservation.

quiz.q: Deleting a post means…
options: Others may already have screenshots or copies
quiz.why: Assume anything posted can persist.

quiz.q: Masked Aadhaar shows…
quiz.why: Safer to share when an Aadhaar copy is needed.

quiz.q: India’s 2023 data protection law is the…
quiz.why: DPDP Act 2023.

lessons.title: Social media and your mind

scenes.text: Every night Riya, 15, in Ahmedabad scrolls until 1 am. Everyone seems prettier, richer and happier.
She feels tired at school, snaps at her brother and stops enjoying dance class.
Her school counsellor, Ms. Kapoor, explains how feeds are designed and how comparison works on the brain.
Riya moves her phone out of the bedroom at 10 pm and unfollows accounts that make her feel bad. After a few weeks she sleeps better and feels lighter.

steps.title: Feeds are designed to hold attention
steps.body: Most apps earn money from your attention. Features like **infinite scroll, autoplay, streaks, likes and unpredictable notifications** keep you coming back. Unpredictable rewards (sometimes a lot of likes, sometimes none) are especially habit-forming. Knowing this isn’t a reason to fear technology — it helps you **use it on purpose** instead of being used by it.

steps.title: Comparison and highlight reels
steps.body: People post their **best moments**, often edited or filtered. Comparing your everyday life with others’ highlight reels can make you feel inadequate. Research links **heavy** social media use with poorer sleep and, in some young people, higher anxiety and low mood, though effects differ from person to person and depend on how it’s used. Using it to connect with friends and learn tends to feel better than passive scrolling and comparison.

steps.title: Signs it’s hurting you
steps.body:
- Losing sleep to scroll; feeling tired every morning
- Feeling worse about your body, life or friends after using an app
- Anxiety when you can’t check your phone; checking dozens of times an hour
- Dropping hobbies, studies or in-person time
- Fear of missing out (FOMO) controlling your choices
If low mood, anxiety or hopelessness last for weeks, talk to a trusted adult or counsellor, or call **Tele-MANAS 14416**.

steps.title: Curate your feed
steps.body:
- **Unfollow or mute** accounts that make you feel bad.
- **Follow** accounts that teach, inspire or make you laugh.
- Remember filters and edits; real skin has texture, real lives have bad days.
- Notice how you feel after 10 minutes of an app — better or worse?

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: For three days, write how you feel (1–10) before and after using your most-used app. Look for a pattern.

activity.label: Hours of recreational screen time on a school day

bands.text: Light use. Make sure the time you do spend is enjoyable and intentional.
Moderate. Check that sleep, study, exercise and in-person time aren’t being squeezed.
High. Many people at this level notice tiredness or less time for hobbies. Try app limits and phone-free hours.
Very high. This often crowds out sleep, movement and friendships. Make a plan with screen-time tools and a trusted adult; seek support if you feel unable to cut down.

quiz.q: Infinite scroll and autoplay are designed to…
options: Keep you using the app longer
quiz.why: They remove natural stopping points.

quiz.q: Comparing with others’ posts often makes people feel worse because…
options: Posts show edited highlights, not real everyday life
quiz.why: Highlight reels distort comparisons.

quiz.q: Which use of social media tends to feel better?
options: Actively connecting with friends and learning
quiz.why: Active, purposeful use is linked with better feelings.

quiz.q: Low mood lasting weeks — what should you do?
options: Talk to a trusted adult or counsellor, or call 14416
quiz.why: Support works; Tele-MANAS is free and confidential.

sources: US Surgeon General Advisory on Social Media and Youth Mental Health (2023)

lessons.title: Healthy screen habits for every age

scenes.text: The Sharma family in Jaipur eats dinner in silence — four people, four phones. Even the 3-year-old watches cartoons.
Mrs. Sharma puts a basket on the table: all phones go in during meals and after 9:30 pm, including the parents’.
The first week is hard. By the third, they’re playing ludo, talking about school and the toddler is singing again.
Mr. Sharma admits he was the most addicted of all.

steps.title: Screen time for little children
steps.body: WHO guidance (2019) for under-5s: **no screen time for babies under 1 year**; for **2–4 year olds, no more than 1 hour a day of sedentary screen time — less is better**. Young children learn language and emotions mainly through face-to-face talk and play. Video calls with family are different from passive watching. When older children do use screens, co-watch and talk about what you see.

steps.title: A healthy screen plan (teens and adults)
steps.body:
1. **Phone-free zones**: meals and bedroom at night (use an alarm clock).
2. **Stop screens 30–60 minutes before sleep**; bright screens and exciting content delay sleep.
3. **Turn off non-essential notifications**; keep calls and important messages.
4. **App timers** with built-in tools (Digital Wellbeing / Screen Time).
5. **Grey-scale mode** makes apps less tempting.
6. **Replace, don’t just remove**: plan a walk, music, sport, reading, a hobby.
7. Teens generally need **8–10 hours of sleep**; adults about 7–9.

steps.title: For parents
steps.body: Children copy what adults do. Model the habits you want, agree family rules together, explain reasons, use parental controls appropriate to age, and keep devices in shared spaces for younger children. Focus on **what** they do online and **how they feel**, not just minutes.

steps.title: When it’s more than a habit
steps.body: If gaming or social media use leads to failing studies, skipping meals or sleep, angry outbursts when stopped, lying about use, or withdrawing from family for months, it may be a problem needing professional help. WHO recognises **gaming disorder** as a condition when such patterns are severe and persist (usually at least 12 months). Talk to a doctor, counsellor or Tele-MANAS (14416).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Check your phone’s screen-time report for last week. Choose one app to limit and one phone-free time to start today.

activity.prompt: My healthy screen plan
items: Phone out of the bedroom at night
No screens in the last 30–60 minutes before sleep
App timer set on my most-used app
One offline hobby planned this week

quiz.why: Face-to-face interaction matters most.

quiz.q: For 2–4-year-olds, sedentary screen time should be…
options: No more than 1 hour a day, less is better
quiz.why: WHO 2019 guidance.

quiz.q: Why stop screens before bed?
quiz.why: Light and excitement interfere with sleep.

quiz.q: Best way for parents to build healthy habits?
options: Model good habits and agree family rules together
quiz.why: Children copy adult behaviour.

sources: WHO guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5 (2019)

lessons.title: Cyberbullying and fake news: be the one who helps

scenes.text: In a Class 10 WhatsApp group in Kanpur, someone posts an edited meme mocking Arjun’s stammer. Everyone sends laughing emojis.
Arjun stops coming to school for three days.
His classmate Shreya writes in the group: ‘Not funny. Delete it.’ Two others agree. She also messages Arjun privately: ‘I’m with you.’
Shreya and Arjun show screenshots to the class teacher, who handles it with the students and parents. The bullying stops.

steps.title: What cyberbullying looks like
steps.body: Repeated, intentional harm online: insulting messages, embarrassing photos or memes, excluding someone from groups on purpose, spreading rumours, impersonation, threats, sharing private information (‘doxxing’). It follows people home and spreads fast, which is why it can hurt so much.

steps.title: If it’s happening to you
steps.body:
1. **Don’t retaliate** — it often escalates and can get you in trouble.
2. **Save evidence**: screenshots with dates, usernames, links.
3. **Block and report** the account on the platform.
4. **Tell a trusted adult**: parent, teacher, counsellor.
5. If there are threats, sexual content, or it doesn’t stop: report at **cybercrime.gov.in**, call **1098** (for under-18s) or **112** if in danger.
6. Look after yourself: spend time with people who care about you; talk to a counsellor or **Tele-MANAS 14416** if it’s affecting your mood or sleep.

steps.title: If you see it: the bystander’s power
steps.body:
Most bullying stops faster when bystanders act. You can:
- **Not join in** — no likes, shares or laughing emojis.
- **Speak up** if it feels safe (‘Not cool’).
- **Support the target** privately.
- **Report** the post and tell an adult.
If you’ve been the one doing it: stop, delete, apologise sincerely, and think about what made you do it — talking to a counsellor helps.

steps.title: Check before you share: a simple method
steps.body:
Misinformation spreads faster than corrections. Before forwarding:
- **Stop**: does it make you very angry or scared? That’s a sign to check.
- **Investigate the source**: who posted it first? Are they reliable?
- **Find better coverage**: do trusted news outlets or official sites report it?
- **Trace the original**: reverse-image search old photos; check dates.
For claims about the Government of India, check **PIB Fact Check**. Forwarding false medical ‘cures’ or communal rumours can cause real harm.

steps.title: Remember
steps.body: Words online have real-world effects. Spreading private images, threats or hateful content can be a criminal offence. When unsure, don’t post.

a.text: A classmate posts a mocking edited photo of a quiet student in your class group. Ten people react with 😂.

choices.label: Add a laughing emoji too — it’s just a joke

b.text: The student says, ‘Please don’t tell anyone, it’ll get worse.’

choices.feedback: Their fear is real, but adults can often help safely.

choices.label: Offer to go with them to a trusted teacher or counsellor, with screenshots
choices.feedback: Going together reduces fear and gets help.

bad.text: The bullying grows. It’s never too late: delete your reaction, support the target and tell an adult.

meh.text: The posts continue. Check in again and gently encourage getting help together — you can also speak to a teacher yourself without naming them publicly.

good.text: The teacher handles it calmly. The student knows they’re not alone. You were the upstander.

quiz.why: Calm, documented action works best.

quiz.q: A bystander can help by…

quiz.why: Bystanders change the outcome.

Add your own comments and share

lessons.title: Talking to parents so they listen

scenes.text: Ishita, 14, in Lucknow wants to go on a 3-day school trip to Nainital. Last year she asked while her father was rushing to work, and the answer was a sharp ‘No’.
This time she waits until Sunday evening tea, when he’s relaxed.
She shows the school letter, teacher’s phone number, itinerary and cost, and says: ‘I know you worry about safety. Here’s how the school handles it.’
Her father asks questions, calls the teacher, and agrees — with a daily check-in call.

steps.title: Why parents say no
steps.body: Most parents’ ‘no’ comes from **worry** (safety, money, studies, what relatives will say) or from **not having enough information**. Many parents grew up in a different world and are protecting you the way they know. Seeing their fear behind the anger helps you respond calmly instead of fighting.

steps.title: The 4-step conversation
steps.body:
1. **Pick the moment**: not when they’re tired, rushing, angry or in front of guests.
2. **Start with their concern**: ‘I know you worry about…’
3. **Use ‘I’ statements**: ‘I feel left out when I can’t join my friends’ instead of ‘You never let me do anything!’
4. **Bring a plan**: facts, costs, safety steps, a compromise (‘I’ll call every night’, ‘I’ll finish my project first’).
Then **listen** to their answer fully, even if it’s not what you want.

steps.title: Words that help and words that hurt
steps.body:
Helpful: ‘Can we talk about something important?’ · ‘What would make you comfortable?’ · ‘I understand.’ · ‘Can I explain my side?’
Hurtful: ‘You don’t understand anything!’ · ‘Everyone else’s parents allow it.’ · Silent treatment, door slamming, sarcasm.
Tone matters as much as words. If you get too upset, say ‘Can we continue this later?’ and come back.

steps.title: When you can’t talk to your parents
steps.body: Some topics feel impossible to raise, or a parent may be unsafe (violence, abuse, addiction). Talk to another trusted adult: relative, teacher, school counsellor. If you are being harmed, call **Childline 1098** or **112** in an emergency. Asking for help is a sign of strength.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Think of one request you want to make. Write: (1) their likely worry, (2) your ‘I’ statement, (3) your plan and a compromise. Practise it once in front of a mirror.

a.text: You want to join a weekend coding club that ends at 7 pm. Your mother is cooking dinner after a long workday. When do you ask?

choices.label: Right now, loudly, while she’s cooking
choices.feedback: She’s tired and busy — not the best moment.

choices.label: After dinner when she’s relaxed: ‘Can I talk to you about something?’
choices.feedback: Good timing makes listening easier.

choices.label: ‘You never listen to me!’ and slam the door
choices.feedback: This turns a request into a fight.

lessons.title: Sibling conflict: fighting fair

scenes.text: Brothers Aman, 13, and Kabir, 10, in Kolkata fight every evening over the TV and the shared phone.
Their mother keeps saying, ‘Why can’t you be like your brother?’ — to both of them. The fights get worse.
Their aunt, a teacher, helps them make a weekly screen schedule and a ‘cool-down corner’ rule.
A month later they still argue sometimes — but now they also team up in games.

steps.title: Why siblings fight
steps.body: Sibling conflict is **normal** — siblings share space, things, parents’ attention and different personalities. Fights increase with **comparison** (‘your sister is so neat’), **unfairness** (real or felt), **boredom**, **tiredness** and **stress** at home. Learning to handle sibling conflict teaches skills you’ll use with friends, colleagues and partners.

steps.title: Fair fighting rules
steps.body:
- **Talk about the problem, not the person** (‘You took my charger without asking’ not ‘You’re a thief’).
- **No hitting, no name-calling, no breaking things**.
- **Take a break** when angry: 10–20 minutes to cool down, then come back.
- **Each person speaks without interruption**; then repeat back what you heard.
- **Find a win-win**: schedules, turns, ‘you choose today, I choose tomorrow’, ask before borrowing.
- **Don’t drag old fights** into new ones.

steps.title: For parents and elders
steps.body:
- **Avoid comparisons and labels** (‘the clever one’, ‘the naughty one’).
- Spend some **one-on-one time** with each child.
- Treat children **fairly, not identically** — needs differ by age.
- Teach problem-solving instead of always being the judge.
- Step in immediately for physical harm or bullying.

steps.title: When it’s more than ‘normal fighting’
steps.body: If one sibling repeatedly hurts, threatens, humiliates or controls another, or touches them in ways that feel wrong, it is **not normal sibling rivalry** — it is harm. Tell a parent or trusted adult. Children can call **1098**. Every child has a right to feel safe at home.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: With your sibling, write a simple agreement for your most common fight (TV, phone, room, chores). Stick it somewhere both of you can see.

lessons.title: Big decisions with family: career, college, city

scenes.text: Rohan, 17, in Hyderabad loves design. His parents and relatives expect him to do engineering ‘for a safe future’.
Every dinner discussion becomes a fight; Rohan stops talking.
His school counsellor helps him research design courses, entrance exams, fees, job roles and salaries, and talk to two working designers.
He presents a plan to his parents. They agree he’ll prepare for a design entrance exam, with a backup option, and review after results.

steps.title: Understand what your family fears
steps.body: Family pressure about careers usually comes from **love + fear**: fear of financial insecurity, of you struggling, of ‘what people will say’, or of a field they don’t understand. Many parents made sacrifices for your education. Respecting that while explaining your choice works better than rebellion or silent surrender.

steps.title: Build a decision file
steps.body:
1. **Interest & strengths**: what you enjoy, what you’re good at (marks, projects, feedback).
2. **Research**: courses, entrance exams, colleges, fees, duration.
3. **Career reality**: job roles, starting salaries, growth, real people you can talk to.
4. **Risks and backup**: what if it doesn’t work out? (another course, a skill, a gap-year plan)
5. **Ask for a trial**: an internship, a short course, a portfolio by a date.
Presenting this calmly shows maturity — and helps you check your own choice honestly.

steps.title: Bring in helpers
steps.body: A **school counsellor**, a respected relative or teacher, or a professional in the field can talk to your parents. Sometimes parents hear the same thing better from another adult. Aptitude and interest assessments with a qualified counsellor can also give neutral information.

steps.title: When pressure becomes too much
steps.body: If pressure makes you feel hopeless, unable to sleep or eat, or you have thoughts of harming yourself, tell someone today — a trusted adult or **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7), or **112** in an emergency. No exam or career is worth your life, and there are always more paths than it seems.

steps.title: Around the world
steps.body: Career conflicts with family happen everywhere — in Lagos, Seoul and Toronto too. Research across cultures finds that young people do best when they have both **autonomy** (some choice) and **family support**. Aim for a decision your family can live with and you can commit to.

activity.prompt: Write your decision file for one big choice: your interest, your research so far, your family’s worries, and one compromise or trial you could propose.
activity.hint: Be honest about risks — it makes your case stronger, not weaker.

quiz.q: Family career pressure usually comes from…

quiz.why: Understanding the fear helps the conversation.

quiz.q: Which makes your case strongest?
options: A researched plan with a backup
quiz.why: It shows maturity and addresses worries.

quiz.q: A ‘trial’ in this context means…
options: A short course or internship to test the choice
quiz.why: Low-risk testing reduces fear.

quiz.q: If career pressure leads to thoughts of self-harm, call…
quiz.why: Help is available 24×7.

lessons.title: Apologies, boundaries and repair

scenes.text: During an argument in Indore, Neha, 16, tells her mother, ‘You’ve ruined my life.’ Her mother goes silent and cries in the kitchen.
Neha feels terrible but doesn’t know how to fix it. ‘Sorry’ feels too small.
That night she says: ‘Ma, I’m sorry I said that. It was cruel and not true. I was upset about the phone rule. Next time I’ll ask for a break instead of yelling.’
Her mother hugs her. They later agree on a phone rule together. Neha also learns to say ‘Please knock before entering’ calmly.

steps.title: A real apology has five parts
steps.body:
1. **Say sorry clearly**: ‘I’m sorry.’
2. **Name what you did**: ‘…for shouting and saying you ruined my life.’
3. **Show you understand the impact**: ‘That must have really hurt.’
4. **No excuses or ‘but’**: avoid ‘I’m sorry, but you…’
5. **Repair and change**: ‘Next time I’ll ask for a break.’ Then actually do it.
A fake apology — ‘Sorry if you felt hurt’ — blames the other person’s feelings.

steps.title: Boundaries with family
steps.body: A **boundary** is a respectful limit that protects your wellbeing: ‘Please knock before coming into my room’, ‘I don’t want to discuss my weight at family gatherings’, ‘I can’t lend money this month.’ Boundaries are not disrespect. Say them **calmly, briefly and kindly**, and repeat if needed. Adults can set boundaries with parents and relatives too — about privacy, money, marriage questions or advice.

steps.title: Scripts you can use
steps.body:
- ‘I love you and I need some privacy — please knock.’
- ‘I appreciate your concern; I’d rather not talk about this today.’
- ‘I can help on Saturday, not on weekdays.’
- ‘When you joke about my marks in front of relatives, I feel embarrassed. Could you stop?’

steps.title: Repair isn’t possible alone
steps.body: Repair needs both sides. If someone repeatedly humiliates, threatens or hurts you, apologies alone don’t fix it — protecting yourself and getting help from a trusted adult or helpline (1098 for children, 181 for women in many states, 112 in emergencies) comes first.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Think of one unresolved hurt in your family where you were wrong. Write a five-part apology. Deliver it when the time is right.

lessons.title: Before marriage: expectations and conversations

scenes.text: Priyanka and Vivek in Pune met through families and liked each other. They talked about movies, food and travel — but not much else.
After marriage they discover big differences: she plans to keep working and move cities for her career; his family expects her to stay home; he wants children soon, she wants to wait three years.
Their cousins Fatima and Jacob, married for ten years, had spent months discussing money, careers, children and chores before their wedding.
Priyanka and Vivek start couples counselling and finally have the conversations they skipped. It takes time, but they find a shared plan.

steps.title: Marriage is a choice and a partnership
steps.body: Whether arranged, introduced or chosen yourselves, a healthy marriage starts with **free and full consent** of both people. Love and attraction matter, but daily life runs on **shared values, communication and practical agreements**. Many conflicts after marriage come from **expectations never spoken aloud**.

steps.title: Conversations to have before marriage
steps.body:
- **Money**: incomes, debts, saving, spending style, who manages what, supporting parents.
- **Careers**: will both work? Relocation? Further study?
- **Children**: whether, when, how many; parenting values.
- **Home**: where to live (with parents or separately), chores, cooking — who does what.
- **Families**: expectations of each side, festivals, visits, involvement in decisions.
- **Religion, food, lifestyle**: practices, drinking, smoking.
- **Health**: physical and mental health conditions, openness about medical history.
- **Conflict**: how each of you handles anger and disagreement.
- **Intimacy and consent**: respect, comfort and that consent matters within marriage too.

steps.title: Legal basics in India
steps.body:
- **Minimum marriage age**: **21 for men and 18 for women** under the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006 and personal laws. Child marriage is an offence.
- **Dowry** — giving, taking or demanding it — is **illegal** under the **Dowry Prohibition Act 1961**. Dowry-related cruelty is a serious crime under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
- **Registering your marriage** (under the relevant personal law or the **Special Marriage Act 1954**) gives clear legal proof needed for passports, visas, insurance, inheritance and protection of rights. Many states make registration compulsory.
- The Special Marriage Act allows marriage between people of any religion as a civil marriage, with a notice period.
This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Red flags before marriage
steps.body:
- Pressure to marry against your wishes or in a hurry
- Dowry or ‘gift’ demands, direct or hinted
- Controlling behaviour: checking your phone, limiting your friends, deciding your clothes
- Lies about job, income, health or previous marriage
- Contempt or explosive anger, even ‘only once’
It is far easier to step back before marriage than after. Help is available if you are being forced: **112**, women’s helpline **181** (many states), or local police and protection officers.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Use the checklist with your partner or someone you’re considering. Note topics where you disagree — they aren’t necessarily deal-breakers, but they need a plan.

lessons.title: In-laws and joint families: a team approach

scenes.text: Ananya moves into her husband Karthik’s family home in Chennai. Every Sunday her mother-in-law comments on her cooking in front of relatives.
Ananya complains to Karthik; he says, ‘That’s just how Amma is.’ Ananya feels alone.
In a calm talk, she explains how it feels. Karthik agrees they are a team. He speaks privately and respectfully to his mother; Ananya also asks her mother-in-law to teach her a family recipe.
The comments reduce. A month later, they cook sambar together. It isn’t perfect, but it’s much better.

steps.title: Why in-law tensions happen
steps.body: A marriage joins two families with different habits, food, rules and expectations. Parents may feel they are ‘losing’ a child or that their ways are being rejected. The new spouse may feel judged or like a guest. Many joint and nuclear families in India manage this well — usually because the couple acts as a **team** and everyone shows **respect**.

steps.title: The couple as a team
steps.body:
- Agree on **key decisions together first** (finances, children, moving out, festivals), then share with families.
- Each spouse usually handles **their own parents** in difficult conversations — it lands more gently.
- **Never mock** your spouse’s family, and don’t complain about your spouse to your family for every small issue.
- **Back each other in public**, discuss disagreements in private.

steps.title: Respectful scripts
steps.body:
- To a parent (by their own child): ‘Amma, I know you mean well. When you comment on Ananya’s cooking in front of others, it hurts her. Could you tell her privately or teach her?’
- To in-laws: ‘I’d love to learn how you make this. Could you show me on Saturday?’
- Boundary: ‘We’ve decided to handle our finances ourselves, but we’ll always ask your advice on big things.’
- Saying no: ‘We won’t be able to come this weekend; we’ll visit next Sunday.’

steps.title: Building goodwill
steps.body: Small regular gestures matter: asking about health, remembering birthdays, sharing chores, involving grandparents with children, appreciating their help. Expect differences and choose your battles — not every comment needs a response.

steps.title: When it crosses a line
steps.body: Constant insults, threats, restricting someone’s movement or money, dowry demands, or violence by a spouse or in-laws is **not ‘family adjustment’** — it’s abuse, and the law protects against it (next lessons). Seek help early.

lessons.title: Fighting fair as a couple

scenes.text: Every night Sana and Arif in Lucknow argue about dishes. It starts with ‘You never help!’ and ends with Arif walking out.
Soon they argue about everything — and stop talking for days.
A counsellor teaches them gentle start-ups, taking 20-minute breaks, and listing all household tasks — including the ‘invisible’ planning work.
They split tasks fairly and agree a signal for ‘I need a break’. Arguments still happen, but they don’t spiral.

steps.title: Conflict is normal; contempt is dangerous
steps.body: All couples disagree. Psychologist **John Gottman**’s long-term research with couples found that **how** couples argue predicts relationship trouble more than **whether** they argue. He described four especially harmful patterns, the ‘**Four Horsemen**’: **criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling** — with contempt the most damaging.

steps.title: The four horsemen and their antidotes
steps.body:
- **Criticism** (attacking character: ‘You’re so lazy’) → **Gentle start-up**: ‘I feel overwhelmed with the dishes. Could you do them on weekdays?’
- **Contempt** (eye-rolling, mocking, insults) → **Build appreciation**: notice and say what you value in your partner.
- **Defensiveness** (‘It’s not my fault, you…’) → **Take responsibility** for your part, even a small part.
- **Stonewalling** (shutting down, silent treatment) → **Self-soothe**: take a 20–30 minute break, calm your body, then come back.

steps.title: Housework and the mental load
steps.body: Arguments about chores are often about **fairness and feeling valued**. Besides visible tasks (cooking, cleaning), there’s **invisible work**: planning meals, remembering bills, school forms, doctor visits, gifts. Write **all** tasks down, including planning, then share both **doing** and **remembering**. Fair doesn’t always mean 50:50 every day; it means both agree it’s fair overall.

steps.title: Repair attempts
steps.body: During a heated moment, small gestures — a joke, a touch, ‘I’m sorry, let me try again’, ‘Can we pause?’ — help bring things back. Accepting your partner’s repair attempt matters as much as making one. Some problems are long-lasting (differences in personality); aim to talk about them with understanding rather than ‘winning’.

steps.title: When to get help
steps.body: If arguments regularly involve fear, threats, intimidation, or any violence, it is not a ‘communication problem’ — it is abuse (next lesson). For ongoing non-violent conflict, couples counselling with a qualified professional can help a lot; it’s a sign of commitment, not failure.

lessons.title: When it’s not okay: recognising domestic abuse

scenes.text: Meena, 29, in Jaipur makes excuses for missing family events. Her husband controls her salary, checks her phone and has hit her ‘only when he’s angry’.
Her in-laws tell her to ‘adjust’ for the family’s honour.
Her school friend Rehana notices bruises and quietly gives her the women’s helpline number and the name of the district Protection Officer.
With support, Meena gets a protection order and stays in a safe place. She says: ‘I thought it was my fault. It wasn’t.’

steps.title: Forms of domestic abuse
steps.body:
Domestic violence is a **pattern of power and control** by a partner or family member. India’s **Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 (PWDVA)** recognises:
- **Physical**: hitting, pushing, choking, burning
- **Emotional/verbal**: insults, humiliation, threats, isolating from friends and family
- **Sexual**: forced or coerced sexual acts, degrading behaviour
- **Economic**: taking salary, denying money for necessities, stopping someone from working, dowry demands
Abuse often starts small and increases over time. **It is never the victim’s fault.**

steps.title: Legal protection (India)
steps.body:
- Under the **PWDVA 2005**, a woman can approach a **Protection Officer**, a registered service provider, the police or a **Magistrate** for: **protection orders**, **residence orders** (right to live in the shared household), **monetary relief**, **custody orders** and **compensation**.
- Cruelty by a husband or his relatives, and dowry-related offences, are crimes under the **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita** (which replaced IPC provisions such as section 498A). Dowry is prohibited under the **Dowry Prohibition Act 1961**.
- Free legal aid: Legal Services Authorities (**15100**).
This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: A safety plan
steps.body:
- Save helplines: **112** (emergency), **181** (women’s helpline in many states), the National Commission for Women’s helpline, **One Stop Centres** (Sakhi) in districts offering shelter, medical, legal and counselling support.
- Keep copies of IDs, bank details, medicines, phone charger and some cash in a safe place or with a trusted person.
- Agree a **code word** with a trusted friend to signal danger.
- Know the safest exit and where you can go.
- Keep evidence safely: photos of injuries, medical records, messages.
- In immediate danger, leave if you can and call 112.

steps.title: Helping someone else
steps.body: Listen without judging; believe them; don’t pressure them to leave immediately (leaving can be the most dangerous time and needs planning); share helplines; offer practical help (a phone, a place to stay, going with them). Respect their decisions while keeping the door open. Men and LGBTQ+ people can also experience abuse — they deserve the same support; counsellors, legal aid and police can help.

steps.title: Children in the home
steps.body: Children who witness domestic violence are also harmed. If a child is being hurt or is in danger, call **1098** or **112**.

activity.prompt: Hard questions about abuse, answered calmly

items.q: He only hits me when he’s drunk or stressed. Is that abuse?
items.a: Yes. Alcohol or stress may be triggers but are not excuses. Violence is a choice and a crime. You deserve safety.

items.q: He never hits me but controls all my money and phone. Is that abuse?
items.a: It can be. Economic and emotional control are recognised forms of domestic abuse under the PWDVA.

items.q: If I complain, will I lose my home?
items.a: The PWDVA provides for residence orders protecting a woman’s right to live in the shared household. A Protection Officer or legal aid lawyer can explain options.

items.q: My family says ‘adjust’ for honour. What do I do?
items.a: Your safety matters more than appearances. Reach out to a trusted person, a One Stop Centre, 181 or 112.

items.q: Can men be victims of domestic abuse?
items.a: Yes. Anyone can experience abuse. Men can seek counselling, legal advice and police help for threats or violence.

lessons.title: Caring for ageing parents: health, safety and rights

scenes.text: Mr. Subramanian, 78, lives alone in Coimbatore. His daughter Lakshmi works in Bengaluru and calls every evening.
One morning he slips in the bathroom and lies on the floor for two hours before a neighbour hears him.
Lakshmi visits and makes changes: grab bars, a non-slip mat, night lights, a pill organiser, a medical alert button and a weekly doctor tele-consult.
She also saves Elderline 14567 and arranges a neighbour check-in every morning.

steps.title: Medicines without mistakes
steps.body:
- Make a **single updated list**: medicine name, dose, time, purpose, prescribing doctor. Carry it to every doctor visit.
- Use a **weekly pill organiser** with morning/afternoon/night slots.
- Set **phone alarms** or a family reminder system.
- Ask the doctor periodically whether all medicines are still needed — older adults often take many medicines, which raises the risk of side effects and interactions.
- Watch for side effects like dizziness, confusion or falls, and report them.
- Never stop or change doses without asking the doctor.

steps.title: Preventing falls
steps.body:
Falls are a leading cause of injury in older adults.
- **Bathroom**: grab bars, non-slip mats, a shower chair, no-step entry if possible.
- **Lighting**: night lights from bedroom to toilet.
- **Floors**: remove loose rugs and clutter; fix wobbly steps; handrails on stairs.
- **Footwear**: well-fitting, non-slip slippers.
- **Health**: regular eye checks, review of medicines, and gentle strength and balance exercise (as advised by a doctor or physiotherapist).
- A **phone or alert button** within reach.

steps.title: Memory changes: when to see a doctor
steps.body: Occasional forgetfulness is common with age. Get a medical assessment if you notice: repeatedly asking the same questions, getting lost in familiar places, trouble managing money or daily tasks, confusion about time or place, personality changes, or poor judgement. Some causes (like vitamin deficiencies, thyroid problems, depression, medicine side effects) are treatable. Early assessment for dementia also helps families plan.

steps.title: Elders’ rights and support in India
steps.body:
- The **Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007** obliges children (and certain relatives) to maintain parents and senior citizens who can’t maintain themselves; claims go to a **Maintenance Tribunal**. It also addresses abandonment.
- **Elderline 14567**: national helpline for information, guidance, emotional support and help in cases of abuse.
- Many banks offer doorstep banking for senior citizens; hospitals and railways may have senior-citizen facilities.
- Help elders keep **nominations**, a **will** and important papers in order; consider a **power of attorney** if they want help managing affairs.
This is general education, not legal or medical advice.

steps.title: Respect and independence
steps.body: Involve elders in decisions about their own lives. Ask before rearranging their home or finances. Keep them connected — loneliness harms health. Short daily calls, visits from grandchildren, community groups and hobbies all help.

lessons.title: Caregiver burnout: caring for the carer

scenes.text: Rashmi, 46, in Nagpur cares for her mother after a stroke while working full time and raising two teenagers.
She sleeps four hours a night, snaps at everyone and feels guilty for even wanting a break.
Her brother in Dubai finally agrees to pay for a part-time attendant; her sister takes weekends; the teens help with meals.
Rashmi joins an online caregivers’ group and starts a 10-minute breathing practice. ‘I can care better when I’m not empty.’

steps.title: What burnout looks like
steps.body:
**Caregiver burnout** is physical, emotional and mental exhaustion from long-term caring. Signs:
- Constant tiredness, poor sleep
- Irritability, resentment, guilt
- Withdrawing from friends and hobbies
- Frequent illness, headaches
- Feeling hopeless or numb
It is common and **not a sign of weakness or lack of love**.

steps.title: Share the load
steps.body:
1. **List every task**: medicines, bathing, doctor visits, bills, cooking, night care, emotional support.
2. Hold a **family meeting** (video calls work) and divide tasks — including money and remote tasks (bookings, bills, calls) for those far away.
3. Use **paid help** where possible: part-time attendants, home nursing, day-care centres for elders.
4. Plan **respite**: regular breaks — a day a week, a weekend a month.
5. Write a simple **care plan** so anyone can step in.

steps.title: Small daily resets
steps.body:
- 10 minutes of slow breathing or a short walk
- Eating regular meals and drinking water
- One conversation a day that isn’t about caregiving
- Saying ‘no’ to non-essential demands
- Caregiver support groups (online or local) — people who understand reduce loneliness

steps.title: Get help when
steps.body: Seek support from a doctor or counsellor if you feel persistently low, anxious, hopeless, or are using alcohol or pills to cope. If you ever feel you might hurt yourself or the person you care for, reach out immediately: **Tele-MANAS 14416** or **112**. Asking for help protects both of you.

activity.label: Box breathing for carers: breathe in 4, hold 4, out 4, hold 4

options: A sign of not loving the person
quiz.why: It affects many caregivers.

quiz.why: Distributed care is sustainable.
